wolof: “Maa mën” : defal ñu gis.
translation: “I can do it”; (then) do it so we can see.

wolof: Àkk àkkum gaynde, song songum bukki.
translation: Charge with the spirit of a lion but attack like a hyena.
explanation: Enthusiasm before action, composure at the moment of action.

wolof: Def ca ba ngay man.
translation: Do it while you can.
equivalents: “Time and tide wait for no man.”

wolof: Fa ñuy tëgge ab xàndoor, deesu fa ñaani njël ; fa ñu koy bey lañu koy ñaane.
translation: Where they make hilaires (an African tool for removing weeds from a field) they do not pray for dawn; it is those who are weeding who pray for it.
explanation: It is in the place where a good idea is put into practice that its value becomes visible, not in the place where the idea was spoken.

wolof: Jabar, doonte ne yeena jéllooy sàkket, ab xer damm.
translation: (In the matter of a) wife, even if you only have a wall of reeds between you, a post can break.
explanation: Even if a marriage seems easy to organise, the future bridegroom will always have to do more and spend more than he anticipates. Tanor owns a large garage and his business is going well. One day, one of his cousins is promoted to head of an important public service. Tanor expects that his cousin will give him the contract to maintain the service vehicles. Some time later he learns that the contract has been given to another mechanic. Tanor makes known his resentment to one of his friends who says to him that he had been too confident and that he should have gone to see his cousin right after his promotion, and quotes this proverb.

wolof: Maa la men deesu ko wax, dees koy jëf.
translation: “I am better than you” is not something which is said; it is shown by action.
explanation: It is not words which count but action.

wolof: Nit la mu jëf la du la mu wax.
translation: A man is measured by what he does, not what he says.

wolof: Soo jiwul, doo góob.
translation: If you do not sow, you will not reap.
scripture: “The sluggard craves and gets nothing, but the desires of the diligent are fully satisfied.” (Proverbs 13:4 NIV)

wolof: Wax yomb na, wànte def yombul.
translation: Talk is easy, but doing is not.

wolof: Jëm ci làmb di bàkku, jóge cay bàkkoo ko gën.
variants: Dem sa làmb ja di bàkku jóge fa di bàkkoo ko gën.
translation: It is better to boast coming from the wrestling match, than to boast on the way to the match.
explanation: Glory comes from the results of action, not from talk.
scripture: “The king of Israel answered, "Tell him: ‘One who puts on his armour should not boast like one who takes it off.’"” (1 Kings 20:11 NIV)

wolof: Pëndub tànk a gën pënduw taat.
variants: Tànk yu pënd a gën taat yu pënd.
translation: Dust on the feet is better than dust on the behind (from sitting).
explanation: Action is better than sitting doing nothing.

wolof: Boroom làmmiñ du réer.
translation: Someone with a tongue will not get lost.
explanation: One should always ask when one doesn't know.
scripture: “Listen to advice and accept instruction, and in the end you will be wise.” (Proverbs 19:20 NIV)

wolof: Tere, tere, mu të, bàyyil mu gis.
translation: Prohibit, prohibit, he refuses to listen, leave him to see.
explanation: If someone refuses to listen to advice, leave him to discover the consequences himself.
scripture: “Blessed is the man who always fears the LORD, but he who hardens his heart falls into trouble.” (Proverbs 28:14 NIV)

wolof: Ku la ne “sangul”, sab taar la bëgg.
variants: Ku la ne “sangul”, sab taar a tax.
translation: Whoever tells you to go and bathe wants you to be beautiful.
explanation: The person who gives you good advice is your friend and has your best interests at heart, even if it is hard to hear.
scripture: “Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses.” (Proverbs 27:6 NIV)

wolof: Déggal ndigal i ñett, bàyyil ndigal i ñett.
translation: Follow the advice of three people, and ignore the advice of three (others).
explanation: A saying of Kotche BARMA. When he said this he was advising people to follow the advice of one's father, one's mother and one's eldest son, and to resist the advice of one's wife, one's slave and one's griot. The first three are motivated by the interests of the man, whereas the latter are motivated by self interest and are only interested in his belongings.

wolof: Bul mere li ci kaas bi, mereel ki ko xelli.
translation: Don't get angry with what is in the cup. Rather get angry with the person who poured it.
explanation: It is good to distinguish between an annoying situation and the author of that situation, between the cause and the effects of a situation. During a meeting in the office of a bank, the president reacts violently against his collaborators because of a situation brought about by the non payment of debts. The secretary, wanting to indicate to him that he should call the bad debtors rather than the employees, cites this proverb.

wolof: Mer, noonub boroom la.
translation: Anger is the enemy of his owner.
explanation: Anger makes you do things that you regret later.

wolof: Mere màndiŋ, mën a waaxoo ko gën.
variants: Mere màndiŋ, dox bu gaaw a ko gën.
translation: There is no point in raving against the desert; better to lengthen your stride.
explanation: It is better to face up to the situation one is in than to be slowed up by the event itself. There are certain things that lie beyond our control. It is better to find an intelligent solution to each situation. See also Proverb 67.
equivalents: “If you gently touch a nettle it will sting you for your pains. Grasp it like a man of mettle, it as soft as silk remains.”
“Don't curse the darkness, light a candle!”
transcriptionNotes: A legacy PDF font maps the printed ŋ to õ in extracted text; ŋ has been restored after visual verification of the source glyph.

wolof: Bul xeeb nit ndax tuutaayam.
translation: Do not scorn someone because of his small size.
explanation: We should not scorn someone who does not seem to be much in our eyes because of his small size or limited means.
equivalents: “Don't judge a book by its cover.”

wolof: Bu sol mànto doon maye daraja, kon géléem du tëdd biti.
translation: If merely wearing a coat gave dignity and presence, then a camel would not sleep outside.
explanation: A camel is sometimes covered with fine drapes which give it a grand appearance, but of course does not change the fact that it is a camel. This proverb is used for someone who carries on in an ostentatious manner to draw attention to himself with the sole intention of impressing people willing to be taken in by his game.

wolof: Bëñ weex na, waaye deret a ko lal.
variants: Bëñ bu weex tàll, te deret ju ñuul kukk lal ko.
Bëñ de na ree, wandey deret anga ca suufam.
Bëñ weex na, nde deret a ko ronu.
translation: Teeth are white but they lie on a bed of blood.
explanation: Beauty is only skin deep. Behind smiles there are sometimes hidden thoughts.

wolof: Bu la taar bi taxa bew, ndax laago du wees.
translation: Don't let your beauty cause you to become conceited and self-satisfied because you can always be struck by infirmity.
scripture: “Charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting; but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.” (Proverbs 31:30 NIV)

wolof: Taar tigi ci jikko lay ne.
translation: True beauty is found in one's character.

wolof: Taarub kanam taarub xol a ko gën.
translation: A beautiful heart is better than a beautiful face.
scripture: “Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair and the wearing of gold jewellery and fine clothes. Instead, it should be that of your inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great worth in God’s sight.” (1 Peter 3:3-4 NIV)

wolof: Rafet kanam, rafet jikkoo ko gën.
variants: Jikko gën a taar.
translation: It is better to have a beautiful character than a beautiful face.
explanation: Good manners are better than beauty.
scripture: “Charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting; but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.” (Proverbs 31:30 NIV)

wolof: Boo xejjatee ci péey ba fa jee ja.
translation: If you are allowed to be at ease in the king's village, don't mess with his wives.
explanation: You should behave properly wherever you are given hospitality and freedom of action.
scripture: “When you sit to dine with a ruler, note well what is before you, and put a knife to your throat if you are given to gluttony. Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.” (Proverbs 23:1-2)

wolof: Deñcin wu ñaaw moo gën jiiñ sab xarit.
translation: It is better to guard your belongings in security, however badly, than to accuse your friend of theft.
explanation: If you do not guard your things well you risk having them stolen, and you will be suspicious of all the friends who have passed by at the time of the theft. Thus you risk damaging your friendships as well as losing your belongings.
scripture: “If a malicious witness takes the stand to accuse a man of a crime, the two men involved in the dispute must stand in the presence of the LORD before the priests and the judges who are in office at the time. The judges must make a thorough investigation, and if the witness proves to be a liar, giving false testimony against his brother, then do to him as he intended to do to his brother. You must purge the evil from among you.” (Deuteronomy 19:16-19 NIV)

wolof: Kuy wékk njoowaan, dangaa yaakaara féexlu.
translation: Whoever puts up a hammock / swing expects to relax.
explanation: When you invest your time and money in something you expect to gain some benefit in the end.
scripture: “The hardworking farmer should be the first to receive a share of the crops.” (2 Timothy 2:6 NIV)

wolof: Kuy xalam di ca jaayu.
variants: Kuy xalam di ca jaayu (barke ba yaa ko moom).
Kuy xalam di ci jaayu barke ba yaay boroom.
translation: The one who plays the guitar should be the first to enjoy it.
explanation: When one does something it is normal to profit from it. It is acceptable to be the first to harvest the fruit of one's efforts.
scripture: “The hardworking farmer should be the first to receive a share of the crops.” (2 Timothy 2:6 NIV)

wolof: Saabu du fóot boppam.
translation: Soap does not wash itself.
explanation: One does not praise oneself. It is for others to make those judgements.
scripture: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; someone else, and not your own lips.” (Proverbs 27:2 NIV)

wolof: Saatu du wat boppam.
translation: A razor does not shave itself.
explanation: One does not praise oneself. It is for others to make those judgements.
scripture: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; someone else, and not your own lips.” (Proverbs 27:2 NIV)

wolof: Boo gisee lëf lëf a tax, boo gisee yàpp, rab a dee.
translation: If you see something, something else was the cause. If you see meat, then an animal has died.
explanation: This proverb talks about cause and effect. Nothing comes about by chance. There is a reason for everything. Every action has its consequences, whether good or bad.

wolof: Baax ak bon, loo ca man a nëbb dafa wóorul.
translation: If you can hide your goodness or your meanness, the reality is that the goodness or meanness is not real.
explanation: It is impossible to hide true goodness or meanness that is natural to a person. It will always eventually reveal itself.
scripture: “The sins of some men are obvious, reaching the place of judgment ahead of them; the sins of others trail behind them.” (1 Timothy 5:24 NIV)

wolof: Lu la réer ci juddu feeñ ci jikko.
variants: Lu réer cib juddu, feeñ ci jikko.
Lu nëbb ci juddu, feeñ ci jikko.
translation: What is unknown to you about a person's origins will be revealed in his character.
explanation: One's habitual behaviour reveals one's hidden origins. The Wolof have a strong belief that one’s character is determined by one’s ancestry. A nobleman will always act nobly. If they find an exception then they will trace his ancestry expecting to find some contamination somewhere in his family line - a descendant who married below his status such as a slave or member of a caste. For any individual about whose origins one knows nothing, it is sufficient to observe his character for a time to know his origins.

wolof: Mbër mu nëbbu bu yàggee feeñ.
translation: A wrestler who hides his skills will eventually be discovered.
explanation: One's character always reveals itself in the end.
scripture: “The man of integrity walks securely, but he who takes crooked paths will be found out.” (Proverbs 10:9 NIV)

wolof: Toxal dëkk a gën a yomb toxal jikko.
translation: It is easier to move a village than change a character.
scripture: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard its spots? Neither can you do good who are accustomed to doing evil.” (Jeremiah 13:23 NIV)

wolof: Ñaaw jikko, rafet jikkoo ko gën.
variants: Rafet jikko moo gën jikko ju bon.
translation: A good character is better than a bad one.

wolof: Sori Sañaxóor taxul ron doon ngeer.
variants: Sori Sañaxóor taxul ron a doon geer.
Ron, sori sañaxóor du ko tax a yem ak geer.
Ron, sori sañaxóor du ko tee di ron.
translation: Even far from Sagnakhor, a ron palm does not become a “ngeer” (Guiera senegalensis)
explanation: An elderly woman is filled with worry concerning her son who has left to look for work in the city. She is afraid he will fall in with the wrong crowd and leave the straight path. A neighbour who has just returned from visiting him in the city reassures her. Her son has found an honest job and still has good manners. In order to calm her he quotes this proverb. [Sagnakkor is the name of the great plain of Cayor, famous for its ron palms. The Guiera senegalensis is a bushy shrub which reaches a height of one to three metres.]

wolof: Jikko dana soppiku jaan walbatiku màtt boroom ba.
translation: Character transforms into a serpent and bites its master.
explanation: The character of a person can be harmful to himself. A certain woman is particularly demanding and quarrelsome. After a certain time her husband sends her back to her parents. Her father, who knows her well, tells her this proverb.

wolof: Xam nit, xam jikkoom a ko gën.
variants: Xam sa waay, xam jikkoom a ko gën.
translation: It is better to know a person's character than to simply know him.

wolof: Wat a gën wef.
translation: It is better to shave your hair than pluck hairs out.
explanation: You should choose the lesser of two evils.
equivalents: “You're between the devil and the deep blue sea.”
“You're between a rock and a hard place.”
“Better lose the saddle than the horse.”

wolof: Benn loxo du tàccu.
translation: One hand cannot clap.
explanation: People who share a common interest need to work together to achieve a common goal.

wolof: Janax yu bari duñu gas menn pax.
translation: Many mice do not dig the same hole.
explanation: It is not practical for several to do the work that only requires one person. When we do not have the same interests, then the results of calling others to help where we could have done it on our own risk being mediocre. This is often used by the facilitator of a meeting to prove that working in smaller groups is more efficient than working in large groups.

wolof: Lu kenn mën, ñaar a ko ko dàq.
translation: What one person can do, two can do better.
scripture: “Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their work: If one falls down, his friend can help him up. But pity the man who falls and has no one to help him up! Also, if two lie down together, they will keep warm. But how can one keep warm alone? Though one may be overpowered, two can defend themselves. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-12 NIV)

wolof: Sanqaleñ yu bari men nañoo watat janax ju dee.
translation: Many ants can drag a dead mouse.

wolof: Wat gaal, ak yëgoo.
translation: Come to an agreement to work together before dragging the boat (up the beach).
explanation: Ideas and actions must harmonize together in order to accomplish something.
scripture: Do two walk together unless they have agreed to do so? (Amos 3:3 NIV)

wolof: Mbooloo mooy doole.
variants: Mboolooy indi doole.
translation: There is power in a group.

wolof: Bu fukk dee gas, fukk di suul, pënd ay bari waaye pax du fa am.
variants: Bu ñaar di gas, fukk di suul, pënd ay bari, waaye pax du am.
translation: If ten men are digging, and ten men are filling in the hole, there will be plenty of dust but no hole.
explanation: When many people are working and many people are destroying it, nothing is going to be done. To achieve anything of importance everyone needs to co-operate and work in the same direction. This proverb is often invoked in organisations to encourage people to work together on the same goals.

wolof: Menn picc mënula yàq ndiiraan.
variants: Menn picc, bu beddiku, yàqul ndiiraan.
Menn picc mënula yàq am ndaje.
Menn picc yàqul um ndaje.
translation: A single bird cannot disperse a flock.
explanation: In a village, all the youth decide to rent their services to landowners who were lacking workers. They put all they earn into a shared fund in order to organise a large party once the harvest is over. At first all went well, but one day Abdou could not agree with his buddies. The field that they had to cultivate was very large and they should have asked for more payment. The others said it was too late and that they could not renegotiate the price. Abdou persists and declares that under those conditions he can no longer participate in the collective work. Someone quotes this proverb to him.

wolof: Yenukati xëddéen dañuy yëgoo bala ñoo jóg.
variants: Yenukati xëddéen, dañuy waxtaan bala ñoo jóg.
Yenukati xëddéen dañuy waxtaan bala ñoo yenu.
Yenuy xëddéen, ak yégóo.
Yenukatu xëddéen dañuy yëgoo.
translation: The carriers of ron palms should be in agreement before they start work.
explanation: It is important to be in agreement concerning the conditions of a matter before beginning.

wolof: Yàlla du la jox njëgu saaku ceeb, jox la doole joo ko yenoo.
translation: God does not ever give at the same time, the price of a bag of rice, and the strength necessary to carry it away yourself.
explanation: God gives to some what others lack, so that we will always be in need of others.

wolof: Béy, bu àndul ak béy ya, ànd ak cere ja.
translation: If a goat is not with the other goats then it is with the couscous.
explanation: A person must choose his companions carefully. He should stay with his relatives and not go off on his own or with bad company for if you have problems which are beyond you then you have no way of solving them. Omar is a boy from a good family and a good student at high school. His best friend, Laiti quit school and lives by his wits. Omar’s father is worried about the bad influence which Laiti could have on his son and advises him not to frequent his friend, citing this proverb. A person should stay with his friends. Going alone only leads to danger and problems.

wolof: Ginaar du am faru siiru.
translation: A chicken does not have a wildcat for a fiancé.
explanation: Mansor found a good way to earn a living through contraband. One of his friends is a customs officer. They see each other often, but the customs officer does not know anything about the activities of Mansor. One day Mansor’s elder brother tells him to be careful of his friend because “a chicken doesn't have a wildcat for a fiance”.

wolof: Ku boot bukki, xaj baw la.
translation: Whoever carries an hyena on his back, the dogs will bark at you.
explanation: If you associate with bad people, others will despise you.

wolof: a. Ñax gu wow dina lakk gu tooy.
variants: b. Ñax mu wow dina lakk gu tooy, waaye it mu tooy dina wallu bu wow.
translation: a. Dry grass will burn wet grass. b. Dry grass will burn wet grass but wet grass will save dry grass.
explanation: A bad person can bring harm to himself, and at the same time harm innocent people around him. One says this when someone has a bad companion, to indicate the dangers of the bad influence; or to a person wanting something but whose character is unknown and who belongs to a group who do not repay debts.
equivalents: “One rotten apple spoils the whole barrel.”
scripture: Do not be misled: “Bad company corrupts good character.” (1Co 16:33 NIV)

wolof: Àndandoo sag maas, diir koo yemal mbagg.
variants: Àndandook say maas, diirook koo yemal i mbagg.
translation: Go with those of your own generation, choosing those who are equal with yourself.
explanation: If you try and keep up with those who are better and stronger than you, you only create problems for yourself, as they will take you past your limits. It is better to surround yourself with those on the same level as you are.

wolof: Béy wu ne, am nag déem.
variants: Béy wu ne am nag déem, (te yaay samag déem.)
Bëy wu ne am na ag déem.
translation: Every goat has its jujube (red date) plant.
explanation: Everyone is privileged somewhere. Everyone has someone with whom he finds favour for comfort, advice, help etc. Massila has a reputation of living comfortably but not of being generous. One day at a celebration a griot sings his praises and those of his ancestors. When the griot has finished, Massila gives him a large note. The griot shows the note to everyone and proclaims he has found favour with Massila, citing this proverb.

wolof: Nit ku bon jikko mat na moytu.
translation: A person of bad character is worth avoiding.
equivalents: “Better be alone than in bad company.”

wolof: Ku am xaritu golo sa ngemb du tag.
variants: Kuy xaritook golo, bu sa ngemb tagee, mu àjjil la ko.
translation: The person who has a monkey for a friend will not find his loincloth caught in a tree.
explanation: The person who has a friend or protector with power has nothing to fear in their company. This proverb was used by Laurent to explain to his son that his fellow student who received his baccalaureate the same year as he, and now had received a scholarship to study overseas was the nephew of the rector of the university. Same meaning as Proverb 59.

wolof: Ku am kuddu, du lakk.
variants: Kenn du am kuddu di lakk.
Ku am kuddu du lakk, walla bu lakkee, di cuune.
translation: He who has a spoon does not burn himself.
explanation: You can avoid doing things yourself if you have someone to do it for you. The person who has a friend or protector with power has nothing to fear in their company. A village is particularly affected by a drought. The majority of the village only eat once a day, and a poor meal at that. From Madhior's the smell of fish and rice emanates. His neighbours are surprised by such abundance. One of them tells the others that one of the sons of Madhoir has just arrived in the village bringing him a sack of rice and some dried fish, and that he is very lucky to have sons who provide for him. And he cites this proverb.

wolof: Gumba du jiite yoon.
variants: Gumba du jiiteew yoon.
Gumba du jiitew yoon.
Gumba du jiite aw yoon.
translation: A blind person does not lead anyone along the path.
explanation: Someone who is not competent should not be the leader. This proverb is often used just before elections to draw attention to those who seek to be elected but do not have the required capacity.
scripture: He also told them this parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit?” (Luke 6:39 NIV)

wolof: Ku mënul, bawoo : lu yàqu yaw a.
variants: Ku mënul, bawul, lu yàqu yow a.
translation: The person who is not competent but does not renounce his place, is responsible for any deterioration which occurs.

wolof: Ku mën te defoo lu yàqu yaw a.
variants: Ku mën lu bare te du ca def dara mooy ki yàq.
translation: The person who is capable of doing much but does nothing is responsible for failure.

wolof: Mën ko, defoo ko, tëlee ko gën.
translation: It is better to be incapable of doing something, than to be capable and not do it.

wolof: Ku mënul dara, du def dara.
translation: He who can do nothing, does nothing.

wolof: Fekkee waral jàmbat.
translation: Being present at an event gives one the right to complain or comment about it.

wolof: Toog di jàmbat te defoo dara du maye dara.
translation: To sit and complain without doing anything will not achieve anything,
explanation: See also Proverb 18.
equivalents: “Don't curse the darkness, light a candle!”

wolof: Fii, kekk la, golo du fi raweeb xaj.
translation: Here the ground is hard, a monkey cannot escape a dog.
explanation: At an animal market, a Peul wants to sell a sheep at any price to Abdou. He speaks highly of the qualities of the sheep and goes so far as to propose easy payments. Ngalandou, Abdou's companion, whispers to him to let it drop, as he is suspicious that the relentlessness of the Peul is hiding something. Abdou responds with this proverb as his way of saying that he is sure that he is not being had. [raweeb = rawe ab]

wolof: Gannaaw ay, jàmm.
translation: After a conflict comes peace.

wolof: Ay du yem ci boppub boroom.
variants: Ay du yem ci boppu boroomam.
Musiba du yem ci boppu boroom.
translation: A conflict is not confined to the one from whom it originates.

wolof: Bëre reenu ñàmbi la, kenn xamul fa muy damme.
variants: Bëre, reenu ñàmbi la ; fa nga ko foogewul lay damme.
translation: A wrestling match is like a cassava root which breaks where you do not expect.
explanation: It is better to solve a problem between people through informal means at the source rather than through official means as you never know how the court/king will decide the matter.
scripture: “I have seen something else under the sun: The race is not to the swift or the battle to the strong, nor does food come to the wise or wealth to the brilliant or favour to the learned; but time and chance happen to them all.” (Ecclesiastes 9:11 NIV)

wolof: Kuuy dawul ; dafa wuti doole.
variants: Xar dawul ; dafa wuti doole.
Mbër dawul, dafa wuti doole.
translation: If a ram backs up, it is not to flee but in order to charge with greater force.
explanation: In a dispute, the fact that one of the combatants is no longer visible doesn't necessarily mean he has given up the fight. It could simply be that he is off finding the means to more effectively attack.

wolof: Fu ñépp di say, ku sayul, yaa dof.
translation: In the place where everyone is having convulsive fits, the person who remains calm is a fool.
equivalents: “When in Rome, do as the Romans do.”

wolof: Soo demee dëkk fekk ñépp di fecce benn tànk defal na ñoom.
translation: If you go to a village where everyone dances on one leg, you should do the same.
equivalents: “When in Rome do as the Romans do.”

wolof: Ku ñépp tëfli, nga tooy.
translation: If everyone spits on you, you will be wet.
explanation: If everyone accuses someone then that person is guilty. One should not speak or act against the opinions of others. An excess of ostentation is to be avoided. If many people make the same bad comments about someone then it will ruin that person's reputation.

wolof: Ku sam xel yeddul, nit ñi yedd la.
translation: The person who is not rebuked by his conscience will be rebuked by others.
explanation: If you do not listen to your conscience, you will end up doing things better not done, and others will rebuke you instead of your conscience, to your shame.

wolof: Màggatum guddi, ku ko gisul mu gis boppam.
variants: Magum lëndëm ku ko gisul it mu gis boppam.
Magum lëndëm, ku ko dajatul, mu daj boppam.
translation: The adult who only acts in the dark, even if others do not see him, can see himself.
explanation: A person who is doing something dubious, even if it is unknown to others, should be rebuked by his conscience.

wolof: Neenug neen, du rey bukki.
translation: Nothing of nothing does not kill an hyena.
explanation: An hyena does not die for no reason whatsoever.

wolof: Nit ku nekk ab tool la, lu ca waay ji, moom la cay góobé.
translation: Everyone is like a field – whatever one sows in it is what one will reap.

wolof: Puubi njugub ci boppam la rot.
translation: The dung of a bat falls on its own head.

wolof: Ku bey sa bànneex, góob saw naqar.
variants: Ku topp sa bànneex, góob sa naqar.
translation: Whoever sows pleasure will reap misery.

wolof: Lu waay góob, gar ko.
variants: Lu ca waay góobe, gar.
translation: The grain that a man harvests, he grinds.

wolof: Lu waay def, boppam.
variants: Lu waay def, mu tees ci boppam.
translation: Everything that an individual does, himself.
explanation: Everything that you do, whether for good or for bad, you do to yourself. Your deeds, good or bad will come back to you.

wolof: Lu waay rendi, ci say loxo lay nàcc.
variants: Lu waay rendi mu nàcc ci loxoom.
Lu waay rendi, ciy loxoom lay nàcc.
Lu waay rendi, ca suba, ba ngoon ci yoxoom lay nàcc.
translation: Whatever you slaughter, bleeds in your hands.

wolof: Ku sóobu tooy.
variants: Bu sóoboo dex tooy xépp.
translation: He who dives in the water will get soaked

wolof: Géej, ku ko xuus, tooy.
variants: Ku xuus, tooy.
translation: He who crosses the sea will get wet.

wolof: Loo ji ngay saxle.
translation: What you sow is what you will cause to grow.

wolof: Ku sumb tooy.
translation: She who does the washing will get wet.
explanation: Any venture requires sacrifices to bring about success. One must be willing to pay the price.

wolof: Tilim dina dem fu saabu mënula dem.
translation: Dirt will get where soap cannot reach.
explanation: There is damage which cannot be repaired. One can be accused, denigrated, and have one's reputation sullied in such a way that nothing can restore your reputation. Malobe is an untrustworthy mason. He has a habit of asking for an advance, then disappearing without completing the work. His family have had to intervene on a number of occasions to compensate his victims in order to avoid legal problems. One day he swindles a man who is less conciliatory than the others. He refuses to accept any settlement and makes a complaint to the police. One of Malobe's previous victims hears about it and he says this proverb.

wolof: Luy daw am na fu mu jëm.
translation: Whatever runs is going somewhere.
explanation: Everything in motion is heading somewhere. This could be a literal object or figuratively a given action which will have a consequence.

wolof: Ku jaaxaan di saw, balaa kenn a tooy nga lóor.
translation: Anyone who urinates while lying on his back will get wet before anyone else.
explanation: Someone who does not listen to advice or an interdiction will be the first to suffer the consequences.

wolof: Ku jaaxaan di colal, ci sa kaw lay dellusi.
variants: Kuy jaaxaan di saw, ci sa kaw lay dellusi.
translation: Anyone who urinates while lying on his back will find it falls back on himself.
explanation: Someone who does not listen to advice or an interdiction will be the first to suffer the consequences.

wolof: Ñaq du feeñ cib taw.
translation: Sweat is not visible in the rain.
explanation: A village organises a collection for the restoration of the local mosque. One of the leading citizens offers 5 tons of cement and 50,000 cfa cash. Another person brings his modest contribution and quotes this proverb.

wolof: Ku la abal i tànk, nga dem fa ko neex.
translation: If someone loans you feet, you will go wherever he wishes.
explanation: The person who pays for something should control how it is spent or used. Abdul Azis and Alassane are reading, commenting on an article in the local paper. The Dakar subsidiary of a large multinational company had laid off one third of its personnel. Abdul Azi asks himself whether this could have been prevented, and Alassane quotes the proverb.
equivalents: “He who pays the piper calls the tune.”

wolof: a. Ku la abal i gët, nga xool fa ko neex.
variants: b. Ku la abal i gët fa ko neex ngay xool mbaa mu nangu ko.
c. Ku la may bët, nga xool fu ko neex.
translation: a. If someone lends you eyes, you will look wherever he wishes. b. If someone loans you eyes, you will look at wherever he wishes, or else he will take them back.
explanation: The person who pays for something should control how it is spent or used. Abdul Azis and Alassane are reading, commenting on an article in the local paper. The Dakar subsidiary of a large multinational company had laid off one third of its personnel. Abdul Azi asks himself whether this could have been prevented, and Alassane quotes the proverb.
equivalents: “He who pays the piper calls the tune.”

wolof: Kuy ñuy diri, doo taamu fu ñu lay jaarale.
translation: The person who is being dragged does not choose where he is made to go.
explanation: The person who pays for something should control how it is spent or used. Abdul Azis and Alassane are reading, commenting on an article in the local paper. The Dakar subsidiary of a large multinational company had laid off one third of its personnel. Abdul Azi asks himself whether this could have been prevented, and Alassane quotes the proverb.
equivalents: “He who pays the piper calls the tune.”

wolof: Lu cin xat xat, xorom ba xaj ca.
translation: No matter how confined a cooking pot is, there is always room for salt.
explanation: Anyone present during a conversation has a right to participate in that conversation. Omar is visiting his friend Sakhir. The family of Sakhir are discussing a matter concerning someone, and they ask Omar for his opinion. Omar politely responds that he is not part of the family and therefore does not want to get involved. They then quote this proverb to him.

wolof: Waxtaan, ñam la, ku ko teewe ca nga.
translation: Conversation is like a meal; anyone present participates.
explanation: Anyone present during a conversation has a right to participate in that conversation. Omar is visiting his friend Sakhir. The family of Sakhir are discussing a matter concerning someone, and they ask Omar for his opinion. Omar politely responds that he is not part of the family and therefore does not want to get involved. They then quote this proverb to him.

wolof: Ku bëgg akara, ñeme kaani.
variants: Ku bëgg akara, dangay ñeme kaani.
translation: Whoever wants (to eat) a bean fritter must brave the hot chili sauce.
explanation: There are often unpleasant or undesirable steps which must be faced with courage and determination before one can achieve one's goals.

wolof: Ku bëgg lem, ñeme yamb.
variants: Ku bëgg lem, war a ñeme yamb.
Ku bëgg lem, dangay ñeme yamb.
translation: Whoever wants honey must brave the bees.
explanation: There are often unpleasant or undesirable steps which must be faced with courage and determination before one can achieve one's goals.

wolof: Ku ñeme yamb, lekk lem.
translation: Whoever braves the bees can eat the honey.
explanation: There are often unpleasant or undesirable steps which must be faced with courage and determination before one can achieve one's goals. [akara is a kind of fritter made with pounded beans and eaten by dipping into a hot chili sauce.]

wolof: Woññ bëñu gaynde, day fekk mu dee.
translation: It is not possible to count the teeth of a lion unless it is dead.
explanation: There are certain people that others do not risk attacking except behind their back or if they have come into a very weak position. It is an act of cowardice. During a reunion the treasurer of an organisation made serious allegations concerning the president who was absent. The secretary rebukes him for his lack of courage and loyalty using this proverb.

wolof: Caga du digleb séy.
translation: A prostitute does not give advice on marriage.
explanation: Someone who is not an participant in something cannot give advice in that area.

wolof: Deñ-kumpa baaxul.
translation: It is not good to be curious.

wolof: Njàng mu ne am na àllarba.
translation: Every course has a Wednesday.
explanation: Every week has one day of rest, no matter what your work.

wolof: Dee du jaas.
translation: Death is inescapable.

wolof: Kenn du gàlli dee.
translation: No one can avoid death.
explanation: No one is exempt from death.

wolof: Deru sëllu wëgg na ndeyam ci teen.
variants: Deru sëllu wëgg na ndeyam.
translation: The skin of a calf watered its mother at the well.
explanation: If you think that it is only the elderly who die you deceive yourself. Parents can bury their children, and a calf can be born and die and its skin turned into a well bucket which brings water to its mother.

wolof: Nelaw tax naa gëm dee.
variants: Gëm naa dee ndax i nelaw.
translation: It is because of sleep that one believes in death.
explanation: Sleep gives us an idea of what death is like and leads us to accept its reality.

wolof: Nit ku nekk a ngoo xasaw néew.
variants: Nit ku nekk, xasaw na néew.
translation: Every person has the smell of a corpse.
explanation: Every person is mortal.

wolof: Ku sag nàkk jeex, nga aj say koog.
variants: Ku sag nàkk jeex, nga wékk say koog.
translation: When you have finished cooking your rice cake you should hang up your calabash spoon.
explanation: When one has used up all one's advantages one should retire. According to Sylla this proverb also talks about our future deaths. One should prepare for death through a detachment to material things, mastery of one's desires and good works.

wolof: Àtte bor ak fey.
variants: Àtteb bor, fay.
translation: The judgement of an unpaid debt is reimbursement.

wolof: Bor du am rakk.
translation: A debt does not have a little brother.
explanation: If you have not paid your existing debt you cannot expect to borrow more.

wolof: Nit ku wóor te doon gor du bari bor.
translation: A man who is sure and honest will not have many debts.

wolof: Bu la ngelaw mayee mbaam, ngelaw a la koy xañ.
translation: What is brought to a donkey by a gust of wind will be taken away by another gust of wind.
explanation: A person should avoid giving the illusory impression of having achieved a result which might evaporate with the slightest change, leaving him ashamed. It is better to be happy with what one has achieved by one’s own efforts while waiting for better.

wolof: Ku yewwu ren dañu la naxoon daaw.
variants: Ñi yewwu ren la ñu naxoon daaw.
translation: The person who is enlightened this year was deceived last year.

wolof: Naxe, ku ca am mbubb, am ca tubéy, mbaxana të la ca.
variants: Kuy nax may mbubb, tubëy ja të la.
translation: You may manage to get the mbubboo by deception, and even the pants and fail to get the hat.
explanation: You cannot continually deceive people without it becoming plain one day. It is not possible to get everything you want by deceiving others.
equivalents: “You can fool all the people some of the time, and you can fool some of the people all the time, but you can't fool all the people all the time.”

wolof: Falleen bët, folli nopp.
translation: Elect the eyes and dethrone the ears.
explanation: We should believe what we see ourselves not what we hear. A ruler should get his facts right before taking a decision based on what he sees rather than on what he has heard.

wolof: Kilifa day folliy noppam fal ay gëtam.
translation: A ruler should dethrone his ears and elect his eyes.
explanation: We should believe what we see ourselves not what we hear. A ruler should get his facts right before taking a decision based on what he sees rather than on what he has heard.

wolof: Ku ëmb sa sanqal, ëmb sa kersa.
variants: Ku yëy sa sanqal ëmb sa kersa.
translation: He who keeps the millet flour that feeds you in a sack, keeps in the same sack your dignity.
explanation: He who lives off you, or in dependence on you, must also defer to you. Dependence is debasing. When a person is dependent on someone, he must show them respect.
equivalents: “Don't bite the hand that feeds you.”

wolof: Lafañ, boroomi mbaam lay faral.
variants: Làggeek boroomi mbaam ay far.
Lafañ, boroomi mbaam lay àndal.
translation: A paralytic always takes the side of the man with the donkeys.
explanation: Advantage is the cement of a union. One always sides with a person on whom one is dependent, even to the point of lying to avoid telling a truth which might not please him.

wolof: Xale bu tàmmul tumuranke du xam àddina.
translation: The child who is not accustomed to deprivation will not attain the maturity of spirit to live a normal life.
scripture: “It is good for a man to bear the yoke while he is young.” (Lamentations 3:27 NIV)

wolof: Bu bëgg-bëgg doonoon jëmm, dina bëmëx boroomam ci kàmb.
translation: If desire had a body it would knock its possessor into a ditch.
explanation: There are those that once they desire something they lose all reason.

wolof: Bëgg a dem taxul a dem, mën a dem ay tax a dem.
translation: The desire to go alone does not result in leaving; it is the ability to go which does.
explanation: One cannot leave every time one wishes to.

wolof: Bëgg-bëgg yee wuute, moo tax njaay may jar ca ja ba.
translation: Tastes are different and for that reason all that one sells in the market will find a buyer.
explanation: Moustapha is surprised that Moses has married Nafi whom everyone finds unpleasant, without grace and not very bright. He mentions it to Abdul who responds with this proverb.
equivalents: “One man's meat is another man's poison.”

wolof: Gaynde bëggul mbuum, yàpp lay dunde.
translation: The lion does not like a sauce of leaves; he lives on meat.
explanation: It is also used to refer to someone with a high social rank who lowers himself to frequent those below his rank. Aissa learns from her friends that her husband intends taking Binta as a third wife. They are all of the opinion that Binta is not attractive or well brought up; in a word unworthy of him. Aissa who is the first wife and knows her husband’s tastes says it is not true, quoting this proverb.

wolof: Xel du namm fu mu xamul.
translation: The mind does not miss the place it does not know.
explanation: A person does not crave that which he does not know.
equivalents: “What the eye does not see, the heart does not grieve over.”

wolof: Béjjénu nag jégeñe na lool, waaye bu ñu laalee du sagos boroom.
translation: The horns of a cow are very close but if they touch it is not because of the will of the cow.
explanation: If it only depended on us, certain things would never happen; but sometimes we find ourselves in the situation where a major force imposes on us a disaster which we never sought.

wolof: Nit ku nekk, juddoom a ko mag.
translation: For every human being there is a superior birth.
explanation: Every person is born with something higher than himself, ie. a destiny in life. David Maranz explains that this proverb means that there is more to a birth or to a person than the physical facts. That is, that crucially important, inherited, spiritual factors greatly affect and even determine all that an infant will become in life.

wolof: Ku Yàlla sànni fitt, doo ko mëna fegu.
variants: Ku Yàlla sànni fett doo ko mana fàkk.
Ku Yàlla sànni fitt doo ko mana fàkku.
Fittu Yàlla mëneesu ko moytu.
translation: The person at whom God shoots an arrow cannot deflect it.
explanation: One cannot deflect an arrow which comes from God. There is nothing one can do to oppose one's destiny.

wolof: Yàq a gëna yomb defar.
translation: It is easier to destroy than to build.

wolof: Alxamdulilaay ju àndul ak coono, amul.
translation: “Praise God” which is not accompanied by trouble does not exist.

wolof: Coonooy njalbéenug njariñ.
translation: Difficulties are the beginning of success.

wolof: Jaaxle, jaaxaan faju ko.
translation: Lying on your back will not solve your problems.

wolof: Mënuñu am dara tey sonnuñu ca.
translation: There is nothing worth having that is not accompanied by difficulties.
transcriptionNotes: The source prints this English rendering in the notes font; its wording has been preserved.

wolof: Bés du ñàkk day sore.
variants: Bés du ñàkk.
translation: Days of want are far.
explanation: Days of want might be far off but they always arrive.

wolof: Juddu bu rafet ndey ak baay, waaye faayda boroom.
variants: Juddu bu rafet ndey ak baay, faayda boroom.
Juddu bu rëy, ndey ak baay, faayda, boroom.
Juddu bu rëy ndey ak baay, waaye faayda boroomam.
Juddu bu rafet : ndey ak doom, faayda : boroom
translation: A good ancestry comes from your mother and father, but you yourself are responsible for your dignity.
explanation: Ancestry may give an individual a theoretically high place but the all important qualities of dignity and esteem depend on the individual imposing himself or herself on others. Meekness is not of value. One cannot count on the reputation he has from his birth.

wolof: Ceddo magul pël da kaa jëkka juddu rekk.
translation: An animist is not older than a Peul, he was only born first.
explanation: Used when one sees through the scheme that someone is bringing.

wolof: Ku dee ca ja ba, yaa tàgge sa bopp.
variants: Ku dee cib marse yaa tàgge sa bopp.
translation: He who dies at the market does his own death announcement.
explanation: When you commit a blatant offence in public, you yourself are responsible for spreading your own shame.
equivalents: “Don't wash your dirty linen in public.”

wolof: Ku la xeexe daw.
translation: The person who uses you to fight will run away (to joke with a friend).
explanation: You are of no use to anyone.

wolof: Coow la ca teen ba, ña amul baag a ko waral.
variants: Xuloo ba ca teen ba ña amul baag a.
Coow la ca teen ba gaaya amul baag a.
translation: An argument at the edge of the well will be caused by those who do not have a well bucket.
explanation: A fight breaks out between two students in the schoolyard. A teacher separates them and asks them what the fight was about. It turns out that Assane had borrowed the pen of Salif and then lost it. Assane often comes to school without a pen or notebook and takes those of others. When the teacher returns to the staff room and talks about the incident he quotes this proverb.

wolof: Njalbéenug toroxte dey neex.
translation: A downfall starts with things that are pleasant.
scripture: “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest— and poverty will come on you like a bandit and scarcity like an armed man.” (Proverbs 6:10-11 NIV)

wolof: Lekkal lu la neex, waaye solal lu neex nit ña.
translation: Eat whatever you like but wear clothes that please others.
explanation: One should always behave in a way that is pleasing to society.

wolof: Bu for yombee, sëgg jafe.
translation: When picking up is easy bending is hard.
explanation: A man of honour should refuse on principle easy and lazy solutions which are a source of corruption.

wolof: La ngeen tàyyi toppleen ko, la ngeen sawar bàyyileen ko.
translation: Follow that which tires you and leave what you are enthusiastic about.
explanation: Don't turn up your nose at those things which are hard, but rather at those things which are easy.

wolof: Daw du may i taalibe.
translation: Running about does not result in disciples.
explanation: People always moving, with no roots in one place, who avoid responsibilities and cares, will not accomplish anything of significance. A teacher who does not sit still will not have any disciples.

wolof: Ku la mage fukki fan, war a xam fukk yoo xamul.
translation: Whoever is ten days older than you should know ten more than you.

wolof: Mag mat naa bàyyi cim réew.
translation: It is important to keep elders in a nation.
explanation: The elders are a source of knowledge which must be preserved. They know the past and present. Their presence in a village is a necessity. The person who listens to them will not stray. This was one of the sayings of Kothie Barma from the famous story of the four pigtails.

wolof: Mag a moom xamam, su ko neexee làlko toog.
translation: The wise elder is master of his knowledge; if it pleases him, he spreads it out and sits.
explanation: It is with respect, patience and politeness that one receives a share of the wisdom of an elder.

wolof: Ku la mag, ëpp lay sagar.
variants: Ku la mag, ëpp la xel, ëpp la sagar.
Ku la mag ëpp la ay sagar.
Ku la jëkka juddu, ëpp la ay sagar.
translation: He who is older than you will have used up more clothes than you.
explanation: An older person is more experienced than you. An older person who has experienced things you have not experienced, and been to places you have not been will always know things you do not know. [lay = la ay]

wolof: Mag toog na séen lu xale taxaw te séenu ko.
variants: Mag dina sóonu di séen lu gone gu taxaw gisul.
Xale séentu fu sori te gisul, mag toog fi mu toog di gis.
Mag dana tëdd di séen lu sori, gone jóg taxaw te du séen dara.
Mag dina tëdd gis lu gune gu yéeg gisul.
translation: What a child standing up does not see, an old man sitting down sees.
explanation: There is nothing so valuable as the experience of years. Youth, in spite of their ambitions and youthful strength cannot understand certain things which are tied to the experience of life, whereas an adult has the benefit of his experience.

wolof: Ba béjjéni kuuy di lëŋaaru, mag ñaa nga fa woon, te mënu ñu ca woon dara.
variants: Man maay béjjén, bi may déng mag ñaa ngi fi, dañu cee mënul dara.
Béjjénum xaaf ba muy woñaaru, mag ñaa ngi fi dan cee mënul dara.
Béjjénu xaaf, ba muy màgg bay wëndéelu, booba mag ñaa nga fa.
translation: When the horn of the ram became twisted, the elders were around, but could do nothing to prevent it.
explanation: The knowledge of the elders has its limits.
transcriptionNotes: A legacy PDF font maps the printed ŋ to õ in extracted text; ŋ has been restored after visual verification of the source glyph.

wolof: a. Mag du gaaw.
variants: b. Nu ngoog xamal nag ne : mag du gaaw.
translation: a. An adult does not hurry. b. It is known that elders don't hurry.

wolof: Waxi mag doyula weddi.
translation: One should not contradict the words of old men.
scripture: “Do not rebuke an older man harshly, but exhort him as if he were your father...” (1 Timothy 5:1 NIV)

wolof: Waxi mag "waaw" la sant.
translation: The words of an elder have the surname "Yes".
explanation: One should respect and follow the words of an elder.

wolof: Waxi mag, weddi, gis.
translation: The words of an elder – deny them and you will see.

wolof: Waxi mag dana guddee àll, waaye du ca fanaan.
variants: Waxi mag day guddee, waaye du fanaan àll.
Baatu mag dafa guddee ca àll, waaye du ca fanaan.
translation: An elder's advice will stay late in the bush but will not pass the night there.
explanation: An elder's advice or warning will eventually come to pass. Therefore one must respect the words of the elderly.

wolof: Boroom karaw gu ñuul ñàkkul dara.
translation: As long as there is still black hair, nothing is lost.
explanation: While one is young there is always still hope. The youth has everything before him and plenty of time to succeed.

wolof: Dox sag ndaw aayul, waaye dëkk cee bon.
translation: It is not bad to live like a youth; it is bad to live it forever.
explanation: One should not live like a youth all of one's life.

wolof: Gone, bu jàqee, tàllal mag ab naqam.
translation: A child when he is at a loss will show his pubis to his elder brother.
explanation: A moment arrives when one is obligated to reveal what one has been hiding.

wolof: Gune dafay seetlu mag.
translation: A child puts an adult to the test.
explanation: Before following his whims a child will carefully observe an adult to discover the extent of his weakness, and behave more or less within the limits of that weakness, be it wide or narrow.

wolof: Xaleel amul bopp.
translation: A child has no sense.
scripture: “Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline will drive it far from him.” (Proverbs 22:15 NIV)

wolof: Gone bu loxo la setee, mu mën a bokk ak mag.
variants: Gone bu loxoom setee mu mën a bokk ak mag ña.
translation: The child whose hands are clean, can eat with the elders.
explanation: A well-behaved child can associate with the elders.

wolof: Aw naaru-góor lu mu mëna mëna daw ñu bàcc ko ab yar.
variants: Fasu naaru-góor, lu mu mën-a-mën daw ñu làbbili ko.
Lu naaru-góor gaaw-gaaw, fàww ñu làbbali ko.
translation: A thoroughbred racing horse, no matter how fast it can already run, is still whipped with a riding crop.
explanation: A little word of encouragement is needed sometimes even for the most valiant. One should not let a person rest on their laurels; that is to say, to stop trying because of what they have already achieved.

wolof: Doomi mbott, ndox du ko rey.
translation: Water will not kill a tadpole.
explanation: When one has adjusted to living in a particular environment or a certain place, one learns how to avoid the dangers of that place. Like the tadpole each person has a place where he is secure and at home. This proverb could be used by a policeman to reassure his wife that he does not take large risks when he frequents the haunts of criminals in the course of his work.

wolof: Joori waay bu mu la tax a sànni say sagar.
variants: Jooru waay du ma taxa wocc samay sagar.
Joori waay, bu mu tax nga sànni say sagar.
translation: Seeing the beautiful clothes of someone else is not a reason to throw away your own rags.
explanation: Never throw away your own clothes because of the beauty of someone else's. Be admiring of someone else's wealth or belongings but value what you own.

wolof: Kiñaan fanqul muur, Yàllaay maye.
variants: Añaan fankul muur Yàlla moo la may.
translation: Jealousy cannot hinder the destiny which God gives you.

wolof: Ku gis nen ne nen-a ngi, waxatumala-ak nenu baa.
translation: Whoever sees an egg says, “Here is an egg”, to say nothing of an ostrich egg.
explanation: One needs to face facts.

wolof: Néegu mbon, ku nekk dana ca fanaan, wànte biddantee ca amul njariñ.
translation: Everyone will pass a night in the room of evil, but there is no value in sleeping in late in it.
equivalents: “You can't stop a crow flying over your head, but you can stop him making a nest in your hair.”

wolof: Nit ku saay-saay a bañ ku ko gëdd.
translation: The scoundrel hates the person who rebukes him.
scripture: “Do not rebuke a mocker or he will hate you; rebuke a wise man and he will love you.” (Proverbs 9:8 NIV)

wolof: Cat, bu la reyul, semmal la.
variants: Cat du reyul sembal.
translation: When ‘evil tongue’ does not kill you, it does at least harm you.
scripture: “but no man can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.” (James 3:8 NIV)

wolof: Ku fecc ba génn ub géew, kenn du la seetaan.
translation: No one continues to watch the person who dances (to excess) to the point of leaving the circle.
explanation: No one is interested in the person who tries to outdo his rivals. This proverb expresses the horror that the Wolof have of excess, of the person who exceeds the norms of the society.

wolof: Kuy bëre yaay daanu.
translation: He who wrestles is the one who suffers a defeat.
explanation: The person who does not wrestle is not worthy even of defeat. Better to try and fail than to not try at all.

wolof: Siiw, du jàmmi boroom.
translation: Fame does not bring peace to the famous.

wolof: Dëkkandoo bu baax a gën mbokk mu sore.
translation: A good neighbour is better than a relative who is far away.

wolof: Dëng ànd ak say mbokk a gëna jub tàggook ñoom.
translation: Unrighteousness which allows relatives to remain together is to be preferred to justice which causes them to break up.

wolof: Doom yomb na, ju baax jaa jafe.
translation: It is easy to have a child. The hard thing is to have a good child.

wolof: Boo bëggee xam luy laabiir, amal doom.
translation: If you want to know what kindness / generosity / indulgence is, have a child.

wolof: Doomu béy, yóbbe na yaayam taq am xaaxaam.
translation: The mother goat was covered with grass burrs because of its kid.
explanation: One accepts irritations for the sake of one's child.

wolof: Doomu ndey dañu mel na baaraamu benn loxo.
translation: Siblings of the same mother are like the fingers of a single hand.

wolof: Gone, lu luppub ndeyam lax-lax, ca lay wuufu.
translation: Even if the thighs of his mother are very withered, a child will always snuggle up there.
explanation: Alfa leaves Mbediene, his home village, to finish primary school in Louga. He is boarding with a friend of his father, where he is welcomed like one of the family. He has everything he needs and his lifestyle there is much better than his actual home. However he is sad and uncommunicative. The mother asks herself what is happening. She discusses it with her husband who replies with this proverb.

wolof: Goro, deesu ko wax dëgg.
translation: One never speaks the truth to one's in-laws.

wolof: Jaboot day boot ñépp, te du wàcce kenn.
translation: The mother of a family carries all the family on her back, and does not let any one of them down.
explanation: When one is responsible for several people one must not neglect any one of them.

wolof: Kéwél du tëb, doom ja bëtt.
translation: If the gazelle jumps over the hedge, its offspring will not burrow through it.
explanation: A child will resemble his parents. He will follow in their footsteps. The good or bad example of his parents will determine the future conduct of a child.
equivalents: “The fruit does not fall far from the tree.”

wolof: Lu juddoo cim tàgg, bu naawul, jaaxal i mbokkam.
variants: Lu juddoo cim tàgg naaw, mbaa mu jaaxal ay bokkam.
Lu juddoo cim tàgg, màgge cim tàgg, soo naawul, jaaxal say bokk.
translation: That which is born in a nest, if it does not fly, its relatives will be worried.
explanation: An offspring will resemble his parents.

wolof: Garab du meññ lu dul la ñu ca gajj.
variants: Garab la ñu ca gajj lay meññ.
translation: A tree only reproduces a bush.

wolof: Janax du jur lu dul luy gas.
translation: A rat only begets something which digs.

wolof: Kenn bëggul ku la sut ba mu des sa doom ja nga jur.
translation: No one wants anyone to be superior to them except for the child that they have begotten.

wolof: Ku la jëkk ci néeg bi moo lay wax ni ngay tooge.
translation: It is he who precedes you into the room who tells you how you will sit.
explanation: He who precedes you (the in-laws) will indicate how you are to act.

wolof: Liibarub mbokk, moo gën kilób jaambur.
translation: Half a kilo of family is better than a kilo of others.

wolof: Nit ku dee te amul doom, raaf na.
translation: A person who dies without children no longer exists.
explanation: One lives on in one's children.

wolof: Reewalal sa jabar ak sab jaam, te yar sa doom.
translation: You should spoil your wife and your servant, but discipline your child.
explanation: Through kindness and generosity you can cause your wife and your servant to become very attached to you, but you should not treat your child that way. A child needs to be disciplined firmly in order to prepare him for the difficulties of life.
equivalents: “Spare the rod and spoil the child.”
scripture: “Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you punish him with the rod, he will not die.” (Proverbs 23:13 NIV)

wolof: Sama nijaay a boot njaboot gi.
translation: My maternal uncle is responsible for the family.
explanation: One should respect one's maternal uncle. If you have a problem with your father you go to your maternal uncle.

wolof: Waajur du moroom.
translation: A parent is not an equal.
explanation: One should always respect one's parents, knowing that they are superior to you.

wolof: Koo jurul doo ko yërëm.
translation: You will have no pity on the child that is not your own.
explanation: One does not take pity on someone who is not their child. Parents are weak towards their children who are sometimes better educated by strangers.

wolof: Jurut du yërëm.
translation: A stranger has no pity.
explanation: One does not take pity on someone who is not their child. Parents are weak towards their children who are sometimes better educated by strangers.

wolof: Doomu-jittle du doom.
variants: Doom jiitle du doom, xaré bu wafe-lë.
Doom jiitle du doom, ay la.
translation: A step-son (a child born from another marriage of your wife) is not a real son.
explanation: When it comes to the crunch, a step-son cannot be relied on. This was one of the sayings of Kothie Barma Fall from the famous story of the four pigtails.

wolof: Geenu golo gudd na, waaye lu ca laal boroom yëg ko.
variants: Geenu golo gudd na, waaye loo ca laal mu yëg ko.
Geenu golo gudd na waaye foo ci laal mu yég ko.
Geenu golo gudd na, waaye lu ci dal boroom yëg ko.
translation: However long a monkey's tail, if you touch it, it will know.
explanation: If you do something to a person, the rest of his kin will immediately know of it. Wali begins to work in an office. He is young and likeable, and his colleagues do all they can to make his start easy, helping him and advising him. To thank them, Wali invites his colleagues to his home one Sunday. At the end of the day, when they are about to take leave, Wali's father expresses his gratitude for the help they have given his son, beginning by quoting this proverb.

wolof: Guy dina jur i dég.
variants: Guy dana jur i dég.
translation: A baobab can produce thorns.
explanation: There can be a black sheep in any family, even if the parents raise their children well.

wolof: Moo juddu ciy géléem nàmp ciy mbaam.
translation: Born a camel, and suckles on a donkey.
explanation: This proverb expresses the fall of an individual which can occur in spite of a good birth. One can be born into a family with a good reputation and still be a failure.

wolof: Jur, mu dee, du yaradal ; jur, mu dund te baaxul mooy yaradal.
variants: Jur mu dee taxula yaradal, Jur mu né léŋŋ, Te fajul dara ay yaradal.
translation: To lose one's children at an early age is not the true misfortune; the true misfortune is to see them grow up to be good-for-nothings.
explanation: [yaradal = indicates the misfortune of seeing one's children die successively one after another at an early age]

wolof: Loo sopp-sopp doomu jaambur, sa doom a la ko gënal.
variants: Lu nga sopp sopp doomu jaambur, sa doom gënal la ko.
translation: No matter how much you love the children of others, you will love your own even more.

wolof: Nag wéq na doom ja, waaye bañu ko.
translation: The cow kicks its calf but does not hate it.
explanation: A child needs to be disciplined. A parent punishes a child, but still loves it.
scripture: “because the LORD disciplines those he loves, as a father the son he delights in.” (Proverbs 3:12 NIV)

wolof: Ginaar dëgg na doom ja, waaye bañu ko.
translation: The fowl treads on its chick, but does not hate it.
explanation: A child needs to be disciplined. A parent punishes a child, but still loves it.
scripture: “because the LORD disciplines those he loves, as a father the son he delights in.” (Proverbs 3:12 NIV)

wolof: Gone, lawtanu yomb la; boo walbatiwul mu law fu la neexul.
translation: A child is like a creeper (calabash vine), if it is not trained in the right direction, it will spread in a direction that does not please you.
explanation: A child needs to be disciplined. All the family have gone out to the field, leaving young Aminata alone at the house to guard it and prepare dinner. When everyone returns they find the house empty and the meal not prepared. Her father finds Aminata playing at a neighbours, and beats her. Her mother rebukes her husband who replies with this proverb.
equivalents: “Spare the rod and spoil the child.”
scripture: “Train a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not turn from it.” (Proverbs 22:6 NIV)

wolof: Waxtaan woo gis diggante baay ak doom dafa war mel na taggtoo.
translation: The conversation which a father has with his son should be like one's last words as though he would soon disappear.

wolof: Xale xamul Yàlla waaye xam na yar.
translation: A child does not know God but he does know discipline.
explanation: A child cannot be left to his natural instincts but he can learn to live by rules enforced by discipline.

wolof: Xaleel poto-poto la, noo ko raaxe rekk lay wéye.
translation: A child is like clay; he takes whatever form that is given to him.
explanation: A child reflects the upbringing he has been given.

wolof: Xalele bañ na loo mu tàmm.
translation: The child hates him who gives it all it wants.

wolof: Yar ca kër.
translation: A good education (only) occurs at home.
explanation: Only a child's parents can bring up a child properly.

wolof: Yar sa doom taxul nga bañ ko.
translation: Disciplining your child does not mean that you hate him.

wolof: Yaru maam du yar.
translation: The education (discipline) given by grandparents is not a real education.
explanation: Grandparents are not able to bring up their grandchildren, as they are not firm enough in disciplining the child.

wolof: Lu jooyloo xaleel a gën lu jooyloo mag.
variants: Jooyu xaleel a gën yu mag.
Jooyi gune moo gën jooyi mag.
translation: That which causes a child to cry is preferable to that which causes an adult to cry.
explanation: There are two possible interpretations of this proverb: (1) One should never hesitate to bring tears to a child by disciplining him. Better the tears of correction as a child than the tears of an adult that come because of ignorance or lack of self discipline. (2) One should never allow a child do something dangerous. It is better to stop him even if he cries than allow an accident which will cause the adults to cry.

wolof: Taawub baay, baay la fu baay nekkul.
translation: The eldest son represents the father when the father is not present.
explanation: This underlines the right of firstborn in Senegal.

wolof: Bala nga wuti jabar, wutal goro.
translation: Before seeking a wife, look for good in-laws.
explanation: Marriage does not involve only the husband and wife, but also the two groups of kinsfolk.

wolof: Dërëm bi génnul gaal gi.
translation: The penny doesn't leave the boat.
explanation: When cousins or relatives marry... the money stays in the family.

wolof: Diggante jëkkër ak jabar, kersa gi warula bare.
translation: There should be little shame between a husband and wife.

wolof: Góor bu takkee tubeyam gaynde la, bu ka tekkee xarum tubaa beer la.
translation: A man is a lion when he puts on his pants, but becomes a lamb when he takes them off.
explanation: This proverb speaks of the ambiguity that exists in the relations between a husband and his wife. In public she must show proper respect. In private there should be an intimacy free of any shame.

wolof: Këll bu ne am na mberoom.
variants: Këll bu nekk ak mberu ma koy ub.
translation: Every calabash bowl has its lid.
explanation: Everyone has his match. There is someone (a spouse) out there for everyone. Astou is a hard working and well-educated girl. However she has a handicap – she has one leg shorter than the other. All the girls her age are already married, and some already have several children. Her parents are worried that she will be left on the shelf. One day Abdou, a handsome deaf man who is mute, returns to the village after a long absence. He asks for the hand of Astou in marriage. Some people are in favour and others disapprove. The elderly Baro cuts short the discussion by quoting this proverb.

wolof: Boo bëggee xam luy muñ, amal jabar.
translation: If you want to know what patience is, take a wife.

wolof: Jigéen, soppal te bul wóolu.
variants: Jigéen ju ndaw, soppal te bul wóolu.
Soppal sa jabar, te bu ko wóolu.
translation: Love your wife, but do not trust her (with your secrets).
explanation: This is one of the sayings of Kothie Barma from the famous story of the four pigtails.

wolof: Jigéen, jëkkëram mooy sangam.
translation: Her husband is the head of a woman.
scripture: “For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, his body, of which he is the Saviour.” (Ephesians 5:23 NIV)

wolof: Aawo buuru këram.
translation: The first wife is the queen of her home.

wolof: Liggéeyub ndey; añub doom.
translation: The work of a mother is the lunch of her child.
explanation: When a mother accepts the pains of housework, the fruit of this appear in her children. David Maranz explains that means that the child directly inherits either benediction or malediction from the mother. It is not inheritance in the physical sense, but the inheritance of spiritual qualities. Much importance is attached to what is called liggéeyu ndey `mother's work', or jëfu ndey `the mother's acts and deeds'. Having a moral, obedient, submissive (to her husband) and pious mother is extremely important.

wolof: Jigéen ju wujjam dee, dara bugalu ko ca.
variants: Jigéen ju wujjam dee, dara soxalu ko ca.
translation: A woman who has lost her rival has no sorrow.

wolof: Sagoy jigéen mooy wujj wu dee ci ngóobte.
translation: The happiness of a wife is the death of her co-wife after harvest (when the work is finished).
explanation: Women do not like polygamy or having co-wives, but it still has certain advantages for them.

wolof: Baay, wékkukaayu yëre la, buy dem yëre bi ci gën lay sol.
translation: A father is like a clothes hanger who wears the best clothes when he goes out.
explanation: A father is the father of all. Whoever gives to him to allow him to maintain his honour and decency is his friend.

wolof: Góor yombul.
translation: It is not easy to be a man.
explanation: The man who is afraid of everything is not a real man. The real man is courageous (in the face of suffering).

wolof: Góor du yox-yoxi.
translation: A man is not afraid.

wolof: Góor-góorlooy taxa doon góor.
variants: Góorgóorlu mooy tax nga nekk góor.
translation: It is by effort that one is a man.

wolof: Góor wurus la, waaye jigéen a koy taxa yegg ci ngalam.
translation: A man is like gold, but it is because of the woman that he attains the highest quality.

wolof: Jigéen doyul a wóolu, ndege lu mu la wax, wax ko sa moroom.
translation: A woman is not worthy of confidences, for what she has told you, she has already told your fellow.

wolof: Jongama benn lal jombu ko.
translation: A beautiful woman is not unworthy of any man (lit. bed).
explanation: A beautiful woman, even from a low ranking or poor family, can marry upwards.

wolof: Jongama du ñàkk laago.
translation: A beautiful woman will still have her infirmities.
explanation: No beauty is perfect. That is to say she may lack other necessary qualities.

wolof: Jongama du ñàkk daaguwaale.
translation: A very beautiful woman is often not complete (in her behaviour).
explanation: No beauty is perfect. That is to say she may lack other necessary qualities.

wolof: a. Bala ngaa fajaan, jëkka wér.
variants: b. Bala nga fajaan jëkka wérle.
Bala ngaa fajaan, wérle.
Bala nga fajaan, fajal sa bopp.
translation: a. Before you heal someone, be in good health yourself. b. Before healing others, heal yourself.
explanation: One should think of one's own faults before criticizing someone else.
scripture: “You hypocrite, first take the plank out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” (Matthew 7:5 NIV)

wolof: Xam sa bopp, moo gën ku la ko wax.
variants: Xam sa bopp a gën nég ba ñu la koy xamal.
Xam sa bopp a gën, nég ba nu la koy wax.
Xam sa bopp a gen ñu xamal la ko.
Xam sa bopp ca teel moo gën nég bañ la koy wax.
translation: It is better to know one own faults than to wait until others tell you about them.

wolof: Ku fóotal mbëtt, roccil bar.
translation: He who does the washing for the land iguana should strip the water iguana of his old skin.
explanation: One should not show favouritism.

wolof: Ndey-ji-seex, njaaxaanaay lay tëdde.
translation: When the mother of twins lies down, she will lie on her back (so that both twins can feed at the same time).
explanation: When you have people under your responsibility, you should treat them all equally.

wolof: Loo ragal da lay gaañ.
translation: That which you fear will harm you.
explanation: The fact of fearing something makes it dangerous. It is the fear of harm which creates the harm of fear.

wolof: Njëlbéen du dara, muj gu rafet rekka mata ñaan.
variants: Njëlbéen du dara, ag muj rekk a takku.
translation: It is not a good start which is important but rather it is a good finish that we should pray for.

wolof: Noppaliku, noppee ci gën.
variants: Noppalu, noppee ko gën.
translation: To finish what you have to do is better than to rest while you are not yet done.
explanation: When you've work to do, do it straight away instead of resting once in a while.

wolof: Niitu ba lakkle.
variants: Kuy niitu ba lakkle.
Dafa doon niitu, faf lakkle.
translation: To play with fire until the house burns down.
explanation: A wife, pampered by her husband was becoming more and more capricious and demanding. She wanted everything she saw and nothing was too good for her. When her desires were not satisfied, she would get angry. Her husband eventually could not cope with her anymore and divorced her. The neighbours commented on her departure, quoting this proverb.
equivalents: “If you play with fire you will get burnt.”
scripture: “Can a man scoop fire into his lap without his clothes being burned? Can a man walk on hot coals without his feet being scorched?” (Proverbs 6:28-29 NIV)

wolof: Jëkk cim pax, sab geen nekk ci biti.
translation: To be the first to get to the hole and have your tail outside.
explanation: This proverbs speaks of those who do not take advantage of being first, when another coming after can profit from the situation. A man wants to marry a girl from the village. Instead of giving presents and hurrying to conclude the arrangements, he lets it drag on. A young man from the village arrives from Dakar with a car and much money, and marries the girl. The first man sighs and laments to his father who quotes this proverb.

wolof: Lu yaq añ, añ la.
translation: What you ate to spoil your lunch is your lunch.

wolof: Cin bu naree neex, bu baxee xeeñ.
variants: Bu cin naree neex, bu baxee xeeñ.
translation: A cooking pot which is intended to be sweet, will smell good when it boils.
explanation: The pleasant odour given off during cooking is the promise of a treat.

wolof: Dof sonnul, bokk yaa sonn.
translation: A fool does not suffer; it is his relatives who suffer.

wolof: Dof ba raw, moo gëna muus ba dee.
translation: It is better to be saved by one's foolishness than to die through cunning.

wolof: Waxi dof, taaw baay gën caat ma.
translation: The first words of a fool are better than his last words.
explanation: The words of a fool start better than they finish.

wolof: Bu la mën-ngawar jayee ba nga mafñàndum saaw, boo fa jógee, loo amati jënde koog teg.
variants: Ku mafñandum saaw, bu déwénee loo bey mu yem cig teg.
Su la mën ngawar jayee ba nga mafñàndum saaw, boo fa jógee, loo bayati jënde kog teg.
Ku namm ngawar tax a mafñandu suñeel, bu ren dee déwén loo am teg lay jar.
translation: If your ability to ride pushes you to the point of riding a porcupine bareback, when you finish you will spend all you have on a saddle.
explanation: There are some things that one never repeats. A good wrestler challenges the national champion despite of the advice of his trainer. He is defeated so quickly that it is ridiculous. One of his seconds quotes him this proverb.

wolof: Sa xaritu noon, sa noon la.
translation: Your friend's enemy is your enemy.

wolof: Xarit dina gën doomu-ndey.
translation: It happens that a friend is better than a brother.
scripture: “A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.” (Proverbs 18:24 NIV)

wolof: Xarit benn-lë, bañ ñett-ak ñenent.
translation: A friend is unique; one cannot have several.

wolof: Wax ma sa ànd ma wax la sa jikko.
variants: Won ma sa xarit, ma wax la sa jikko.
translation: Show me your friend, and I will tell you your character.
equivalents: “A man is known by the company he keeps.”

wolof: Garab gu dul meññ du am yoon.
variants: Garab gu dul tàbbal ay doom doo am aw yoon.
translation: There is no path to a fruitless tree.
explanation: People will cease to visit someone who is not generous. This is a saying of Kotche BARMA. The king (Damel Daw DEMBA) looked down on his subjects whom he feared and despised at the same time. One day he wanted to go to war against the King of Baol. He alerted his warriors but no one responded. Perplexed he asked his royal council to explain but no one dared to respond to him. Finally he called Kotche BARMA who responded to his question with this saying. He wanted the king to understand that to receive the loyalty and devotion of his people he must love his people and treat them with respect. The proud king can only expect to be abandoned in times of trouble.

wolof: Ëllëg, ëllëgu Yàlla la.
variants: Ëllëg, ëllëg gu Yàlla la.
translation: The future belongs to God.
explanation: Only God knows what the future will bring.

wolof: Ëllëg du añ, du reer, waaye dees na ko sédd.
variants: Ëllég du añ du reer, waaye jar na sédd.
Ëllëg du añ, du reer, waaye mat nay sédd.
Ëlleg du añ, du reer, waaye lu mata sédd di leen yaxanal.
translation: Tomorrow does not have lunch or dinner, but one should put aside its ration.
explanation: You must save for the needs of the future. Prudence invites us to have foresight.
equivalents: “Save your pennies for a rainy day.”

wolof: Bul di njëkkee li mujjee.
translation: Don't put first what should be last.
equivalents: “Don't put the cart before the horse.”

wolof: Dëkk gaar ba taxul a bare i gan.
translation: To live at a bus station is not a reason to have many visitors.
explanation: Ndiasse works in a bank, His companions believe that they can count on him to obtain loans for them. He is bombarded with requests from his friends and cousins. In order to make them understand he cannot satisfy their demands he quotes this proverb.

wolof: Ëkk nit la.
translation: That stump is a person.
explanation: Beware of talking in the presence of a child as he will report it to someone else.

wolof: Ku aye, wol sa moome.
translation: Whoever's turn it is should do the pounding the turn demands.
explanation: Each day is yours to do with as you wish. While he reigns a King can do what he wishes. But his reign will one day come to an end, and another takes his place. Whatever he does whether good or bad, it will surely pass. This proverb is usually used in reference to a ruler or authority.

wolof: Ku bërewul itam, ñu bëre daanu ci sa kaw.
translation: As for him who does not wrestle, those who do wrestle will fall on top of you.
explanation: An honest person who does not engage in dubious activities can still get caught up with those who do.

wolof: Ku mënoona dog sa bopp, su dogee sa baaraam rekk, na nga fab sa baaraam, daw te gërëm Yàlla.
translation: If someone could have cut off your head and he only cuts off a finger, take your finger, flee and thank God.

wolof: Ku njëriñ jot, nga yàgg fa.
translation: Wherever you find that which is useful, spend a long time there.

wolof: Lu bukki om-a-om, mën naa bëreek béy.
translation: No matter how wasted a hyena is, he can still fight with a goat.
explanation: There are certain evil people, no matter how weak they are, who can ruin the affairs of someone who is good.

wolof: Néew na a gën nañu ko bàyyi.
translation: It is better to have a small amount than to refuse it.

wolof: Neexum ngont, xam fooy fanaanee ko gën.
translation: It's good to have a good afternoon but it's better to know where you are going to spend the night.
explanation: As good as the moment you are having is, you should ensure that the follow up is all set in place.

wolof: Petax am rab la.
translation: The pigeon of the animal is there.
explanation: A Senegambian phrase, used to stop a conversation concerning one who is absent, when suddenly there appears somebody who is likely to let him know what was said. M. Dard considers this proverb a proof that Negroes formerly used carrier pigeons. It may, however, allude to the mythical pigeon that whispered in the Prophet's ear.

wolof: Ndigg toq moo gën taati neen.
