translation: A small cache-sex is better than a bare backside.

wolof: Faru lawbe gënug neen.
translation: It is better to have a fiancé who is a lawbe than to have nothing at all.
explanation: [Lawbe are generally looked down on in Senegal, therefore not considered to be a good choice for a marriage partner.]

wolof: Coqam a gën këmm,
translation: To have a small amount of food is better than nothing.
explanation: [coqum and këmm are sounds that go with eating. Coqum is the smacking sound of moisture in the mouth. Këmm is the absence of sound.]

wolof: Sagaru tubéy a gën taati neen.
translation: Ragged trousers are better than a bare backside.

wolof: Néew na moo gën dara.
translation: A little is better than nothing.

wolof: Reer ci goloo gën fande.
translation: It is better to eat dinner with monkeys than go hungry all night.

wolof: Fas wu làpp a gën fas wu réer.
translation: It is better to have an emaciated horse than one that is lost.

wolof: Rendi bu ñaaw a gën médd.
translation: An ugly slaughter is better than allowing the animal to die of natural causes.
explanation: [In Islam it is forbidden to eat meat which has not been ritually slaughtered. Thus any animal which dies of accidental or natural causes cannot be eaten.]

wolof: Picc, la muy wax ci banqaasu garab, du ko wax ci loxol gone.
translation: What the bird says/sings high in a tree it will not say in the hands of a child.
explanation: Someone cries “thief” in a crowd at Kermel Market. The police come and arrest Abdou in spite of his protests. At the police station he is forced to confess. However, when the case comes to court he proclaims his innocence. When the judge asks why he confessed he quotes this proverb.

wolof: Wàcc, daanoo ci gën a gaaw.
translation: When it comes to getting down, letting yourself fall is the fastest (method).
explanation: When it comes to telling the truth say it frankly. One should get straight to the point, and head straight for the goal.

wolof: Tànk ci suuf, jaan ci suuf, fu ñu jaar daje.
translation: The feet are on the ground, and the snake is also on the ground, so inevitably they will meet.
explanation: Abdou was greatly offended by Alassane. He sought to meet him to make him accountable for his offence but Alassane continually avoided him. Abdou therefore asked a relative of Alassane's to pass on this proverb.

wolof: Ana golo aka xastey daar-daar ?
variants: Ana goloo ka xastey daar-daar ?
Ana golo ak a xaste ay daar-daar ?
translation: What monkey would mock (another) for the calluses?
explanation: Bounama is in the process of disciplining his son with a stick. Bounama's father arrives and observes the scene. The child flees. The old man asks his son the reason for the correction. Bounama explains that he was sent home from school for copying several times. His father reminds Bounama that he too did the same things when he was his age, and smiling adds this proverb.

wolof: Bóli gu dog, doktoor amu ca pexe.
variants: Bóli gu dog, tiiñ nab doktoor.
Bóli gu dog tiiñ na ab doktoor.
Bóli gu dog, doktoor mënu ci dara.
Put gu dog tiiñ na doktoor.
translation: A doctor does not have a solution for a throat which is cut.
explanation: There are problems which are beyond solution. This proverb is used to rebuke the person who has allowed a situation to get to a point where it is beyond solving, and also to encourage people to avoid allowing things to get that far.

wolof: War fasu gattax ba am fasu weñ.
variants: Dawal fasu gattax ba am fasu weñ.
translation: Ride a horse of millet stalks until you have an iron horse.
explanation: Make do with what one has until one has something better.

wolof: Goloo la gëna xam kër gu barey xaj.
variants: Golo xammee na kër gu am xaj.
translation: The monkey knows better than you the house with many dogs.
explanation: David is a real womanizer. All the village are talking about him and all the heads of family complain about his behaviour. Moussa makes a true remark, “Why does David not frequent the home of Maissa?” Everyone there exclaims and says this proverb because everyone knows that Maissa is particularly suspicious and vindictive.

wolof: Nen du bëreek doj.
variants: Nen du wuréek u doj.
Nen du wure ak doj.
translation: An egg should not wrestle with a rock.
explanation: A person should not fight against someone or something which is much stronger than he is.

wolof: Ku aj a gën a bañ ku séenu kaw.
variants: Ku aj a gën a bañ ku téen.
translation: If you store your valuables under the ceiling you do not want anyone to look up.
explanation: The person who done some offence does not want someone announcing what he has done to others.

wolof: Ñetti lonk, benn du ca fàq : lunku jigéen, lunku buurfari, lunku jinne.
variants: Ñett ñu lunku duñu fàq : lunkum jigéen, lunkum buurfari, lunkum malaaka.
translation: There are three attachments which are difficult to break: the attachment of a woman, the attachment of a great king, and the attachment of a genie.

wolof: Su Mbul bañee, Làmbaay nangu.
variants: Su buur bañee lambaay nangu.
translation: If the king of Mboul refuses, the king of Làmbaye will accept.
explanation: You can refuse something, and your peers accept it, or certainly hate you while others like you. A farmer goes to a business man to sell a portion of his millet crop. The business man offers a price which the farmer considers too low. They discuss the price but each holds his position. Someone observing the discussion whispers this proverb in the ear of the farmer to suggest to him that he try another business man. [Mboul was the capital of the ancient Wolof kingdom of Cayor and Làmbaye was the capital of ancient Baol. The two kingdoms were rivals.]

wolof: Xalam demoon na bay neex, buum ya dog.
variants: Xalam demoon na bay neex, buum ga dog.
Xalam demoon na bay neex, buum ya dogandoo.
translation: The sound of the xalam was so beautiful but the strings broke all of a sudden.
explanation: Sometimes some business will proceed to the point of bringing hope, then that hope will vanish. It is the same also with people.
equivalents: “Don't count your chickens before they hatch.”

wolof: Xarum waay, gayndeg waay.
variants: Gayndeg waay, xarum waay.
translation: One is at the same time the sheep of someone and the lion of someone else.
explanation: In whatever domain of life there are always those who surpass you (which invites humility) and those whom you surpass (a reason for consolation, not for self-deprecation). The proverb is illustrated by a story recounted by Mamousse Diagne. There was once a man in such dire poverty that he was on the verge of committing suicide. He was in such dire straits that all he had to wear as he walked to the edge of a cliff to throw himself off was a loincloth in rags. The moment he was about to jump off he heard someone whispering from the bushes nearby. The man was completely naked and obliged to hide in the bushes. He asked the other man in the name of God, to give him his loincloth before he jumped off the cliff. On realising that he wasn't the most miserable creature on earth, the first man reconsidered his decision to kill himself.

wolof: Bul sa loxo ubbiku ndax nangu te téju ndax maye.
translation: Do not let your hands be open to receive and closed to give.
scripture: “There will always be poor people in the land. Therefore I command you to be open-handed towards your brothers and towards the poor and needy in your land.” (Deuteronomy 15:11 NIV)

wolof: Ku bëgg yaa baax, dangay maye sa alal.
translation: Whoever wants to hear “you are good” should give of his wealth.

wolof: Ku la ne : « mayeel sa alal », sa ngërëm la bëgg.
translation: The person who tells you to give of your wealth wants you to be praised.

wolof: Taaru, tabee ko gën.
translation: It is better to be generous than beautiful.

wolof: Yéwén : ci sa alal.
translation: Be generous, but only with your own belongings.

wolof: Bu joxe doon tax a ñàkk, kon ku watu doo sëq.
translation: If giving away were to bring us to poverty, one who shaves would never get his hair back.
explanation: Giving to others will not make you become poor.

wolof: Mayee lu baax ci kër laa njëkkee.
translation: Good giving begins at home.

wolof: Mayu nangu baaxul.
translation: One who gives and then takes back is bad.

wolof: Mbaam du jur ci kanam nit.
translation: A donkey does not give birth in front of people.
explanation: Used when one is prepared to give someone something, but not in the middle of a crowd of people.

wolof: Am bukki yomb na, waaye bukki buy xalam a jafe.
translation: It is easy to capture an hyena, but it is another thing to capture an hyena that plays the guitar.
explanation: It is good to have high goals but all the same there are limits to what one can achieve.

wolof: Boo ma jàppee fu Yàlla nekkul, rey ma.
translation: If you can catch me somewhere where God is not, then kill me.
explanation: This is given as a response to someone who threatens you.

wolof: Bu Yàlla amulwoon, nit du am.
translation: If there were no God there would be no people.

wolof: Buur Yàlla day nattub jaamam.
translation: God the King tests his servants.
scripture: “Remember how the LORD your God led you all the way in the desert these forty years, to humble you and to test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep his commands.” (Deuteronomy 8:2 NIV)

wolof: Koo yaakaar, Yàlla la yaakaar.
translation: He who hopes, hopes in God.
explanation: Our hopes return to God, Lord of everyone, everything, everywhere.

wolof: Ku Yàlla may mu am.
translation: He to whom God gives, will have.

wolof: Ku wóolu Yàlla, dinga wér.
translation: He who trusts in God will succeed.

wolof: Lëkkaayu Yàlla, xalangu du ko dindi.
translation: Rolling around on the ground will not remove the wraparound skirt God has placed on you.
explanation: A person cannot remove what nature has given him.

wolof: Lu jot Yàlla def ko.
translation: Whatever happens, God has done it.

wolof: Lu am Yàllaa !
translation: Whatever is, is because of God.

wolof: Lu dul Yàlla, ag neen la.
translation: What is not of God, is nothing.
scripture: “Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labour in vain.” Psa 138:1 NIV

wolof: Lu waay jaay fa Yàlla, fekk fa njëgam.
translation: What a person sells to God, he will find a price there.
explanation: God will repay every man according to his deeds. Therefore we should do good.

wolof: Xam Yàlla ca la nga weesu.
translation: Know God through what you have experienced in the past.
explanation: It is through past life experiences that one discovers God.

wolof: Yàlla rekk moo moom baax.
translation: God alone owns goodness.
explanation: If I'm good, it's from God.
scripture: “"Why do you ask me about what is good?" Jesus replied. "There is only One who is good. If you want to enter life, obey the commandments."” (Matthew 19:17 NIV)

wolof: Yàlla du teg nit lu mu àttanul.
translation: God does not place on a person what he is not capable of bearing.
scripture: “No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, he will also provide a way out so that you can stand up under it.” 1 Cor 11:14 NIV

wolof: Yàlla amul palanteer bu mu naan la tollu ma foofu ma jox la.
translation: God does not have a window through which He says come here and I will give to you.
explanation: That which God gives comes through the intermediary of another person.

wolof: Yàlla bindul ku mu dul rey waaye am na ñu mu dul toroxal.
translation: God has not created anyone whom he does not kill, but there are those whom he does not humiliate.
explanation: The elect of God will die just like everyone else, but God looks after their integrity. He will never abandon them.

wolof: Yàlla, gémmiñ gu mu xotti sànni ca ab tib.
variants: Gémmiñ gu Yàlla sàkk sànni ci pepp.
translation: God places grain in every mouth that He creates.
explanation: God feeds all his creatures.

wolof: Yàlla buy séddale, ñatt, ñatti nit, dey jox ñaar kenn, jox benn kenn, ne ka ca des topp leen lu rot nga for.
translation: When God divides something into three parts for three people, He gives two parts to one person, one part to the second, and allows the third to follow the other two and collect what falls from their hands.
explanation: This proverb speaks of the inequality of the lot of people in the world. It is enough to note the acts of God's wisdom without judging.

wolof: Jaam ak pexeem, Yàllaak dogalam.
variants: Jaam ak yéeneem, Yàlla ak dogalam.
Nit ay bëgg-bëggam, Yàlla ak dogalam.
translation: Man and his plans and desires; God with his decisions.

wolof: Soo xamoon li lay yoot, nga bàyyi li ngay yoot te daw.
variants: Ku xamoon li lay yoot, nga bàyyi li ngay yoot te daw.
Ku xamoon li lay dàq, nga bàyyi li ngay dàq.
translation: If you knew what was stalking you, you would abandon what you were stalking and flee.
explanation: This is a warning to those who live in the world as though God does not exist and there is no coming judgement.
scripture: “Just as man is destined to die once, and after that to face judgment,” (Hebrews 9:27 NIV)

wolof: Lu la Yàlla jox, waruloo ko xeeb.
variants: Nit lu ko Yàlla jox waru ko xeeb.
translation: You should not despise what God deals you.

wolof: Taal bu Yàlla taal, sànni cag matt a gën fey ko.
variants: Taal bi Yàlla taal, sànni ci matt moo gën di ko jéem fey.
Taal bu Yàlla taal, sànni cag matt a gëna jéem koo fey.
translation: It is better to throw wood on the fire which God lights than to try and put it out.
explanation: You will only tire yourself if you try and fight what God has put in place. Acts 5:33-39

wolof: Duñuy fàttaliku laaxu daaw/démb, cifaay ba tax.
variants: Laaxub daaw, bu ñu ko dee nettali cafaay laa taxe.
Laaxub daaw, bu ñu koy nettali, cifaay laa tax.
translation: If they remember/talk about yesterday's millet porridge, it is because of the sauce which is added to give it flavour (usually curdled milk).
explanation: When people remember events of the past, it is because of significant events that occurred then.

wolof: Donn sa tabaxub baay, donn ngërëmam a ko gën.
translation: It is better to inherit the gratitude of your father than his building.

wolof: Ku iñaanul ne Yàllaak diw.
translation: He who is not jealous should say, “It is because of God and so-and-so.”
explanation: We owe gratitude to someone for whatever we have. After thanking God, we should also thank the person through whom the blessing has come.

wolof: Ku gërëmul nit ñi doo gerëm Yàlla.
translation: The person who is not grateful to man will not be grateful to God.
explanation: If one is not grateful for benefits which are received from people whom he can see, he certainly will not be grateful for blessings which he receives from God whom he cannot see.

wolof: Lu mana am, gërëm Yàllaak sa ndey.
translation: Whatever happens, thank God and your mother.
explanation: Without God and one’s mother a person would be nothing.

wolof: Purux du gërëm ñamu daaw.
translation: The throat is not grateful for last year's meal.
explanation: Favours of the past are quickly forgotten by an ungrateful person. Said to a person who has forgotten what others have has done for him in the past; one who isn't grateful to those who have helped him a long time ago.

wolof: Bu lëg lekkee aloom, na ko gërëme coy.
variants: Lëg su lekkee aloom war na koo gërëme coy.
Bu lëg mosee alom, na ko gërëme coy.
Bu lëg ñamee aloom, na ko gërëme coy.
translation: When the hare eats jackal berries, it should thank the parrot.
explanation: When one enjoys something, one should be grateful to the person who made it possible. As a result of a strike, the employees had obtained rise in salary. One of the workers, who had not participated in the strike was very happy. A union representative remarked to him that he had benefited from advantages won by others and quoted this proverb.

wolof: Su tan gore woon, bu ñuy gubal mbaam, mu ëpp caw say.
variants: Tan dafa gàtt xel nde kon bunuy gubal mbaam mu ëpp caw say.
Bu tan gore woon, bu nuy gubali mbaam kenn du ko ca jiitu.
translation: If the vulture was honest, when they go to cut grass for the donkey, it would cut the largest sheath.
explanation: This proverb has the same meaning as Proverb 328. [Wolof do not eat donkey meat. A dead donkey will be left for the vultures.]

wolof: Bëgge du mat, ngor mat.
variants: Mbëgge du mat, ngor mat.
translation: One cannot have at the same time complete greed and perfect honesty.
explanation: According to the Wolof one must either master one's desires or else fall into dishonesty. There is no compromise between these two extremes.

wolof: Ku bëgge tax a xar sab dënn, ñaw ko dina la jaaxal.
translation: If greed causes you to cleave your chest, sewing it up again will be difficult.
explanation: If greed causes you to enter into wrongdoing, if you are not careful you will not escape from this.

wolof: Ku dikkoon, da nga demati.
translation: Whoever has arrived will eventually leave.

wolof: Lu gan sonal-sonal, dina ñibbi.
translation: No matter how annoying a guest is, he will eventually go home.

wolof: Su gan ŋàbboo, dëkk a ko ca bàyyi.
translation: If a guest complains it is because he has abandoned his village.
explanation: If a guest complains it is because he is well established.
transcriptionNotes: A legacy PDF font maps the printed ŋ to õ in extracted text; ŋ has been restored after visual verification of the source glyph.

wolof: Gan du yewwiy béy.
variants: Gan du yewwi bëy.
translation: A stranger does not let out the goats.
explanation: A stranger has no business becoming involved in family affairs.

wolof: Ginaar gu bu ñu gaddu, xamul yoon wu sore.
variants: Ginaar gu ñu gàddu xamul yooni je bu sore.
translation: The fowl you are carrying on your shoulder does not know how long the road is.
explanation: If you live off someone else you should be careful not to be wasteful.

wolof: Tànk du tàmm gudd, gàtt.
translation: Feet that have the habit of wandering cannot give it up all of a sudden.
explanation: It's very difficult to get rid of a habit.

wolof: Kanam du kaso, waaye koo ca tëj mu xam ko.
translation: The face is not a prison but if you close someone in it, he'll know about it.
explanation: Your face can show that you are mad at someone.

wolof: Xol du wóom ba ñu koy bës.
translation: The heart is not a knee that you can massage at will.
explanation: Some pains in life are difficult to soothe.

wolof: Lu jebbi ci xol, focci ci jë.
variants: Lu meññ ci xol, jebbi ci xar-kanam.
translation: That which germinates in the heart will sprout a head on the forehead.
explanation: That which is happening in the heart will be evident in a person's face.

wolof: Ker, kenn du ca mbaar.
translation: No one builds a shelter over shade.
explanation: No one helps someone who is capable of doing it himself, and leaves the person who needs help.

wolof: Ku amagul ab tool, maneesu koo may ab liggéey.
translation: Whoever does not have a field cannot be helped with the offer of helping hands.
explanation: He who does not try anything cannot be helped.

wolof: Ndimbal, na ca fekk loxol boroom.
variants: Ndimbal na ca fekk loxol boroom, (ba mu des lol liir mbaa lol néew).
translation: Help should find that the person being helped is already trying to help himself.
explanation: It is hard to help someone who is not making any effort himself. Before asking for help one should already be actively working on that which he desires help with.

wolof: Doomu ñey bu ko ñaanal mu réy, ñaanal ko mu wér to gudd fan.
variants: Ñey wu ndaw, ñaanal ko fan wu gudd te bañ koo ñaanal réy.
translation: Do not pray that a baby elephant will become huge, but rather that he will have a long and healthy life.
explanation: An elephant will by nature become large so there is no point praying for this. Any help given to an individual should be directed at his needs, not based on what the helper would like to do.

wolof: Peccum liir bu neexee, ndey jaa jàpp ca wagg ya.
variants: Peccum liir bu neexee, ndey jaa téyé ca wagg ya di yëngal.
Peccum liir, bu neexee, ndeyam a téye ca tànk ya.
Su peccum liir neexee, ndey jaa téye ca wagg ya.
translation: If the dance of a baby is pleasant it is because his mother is holding his shoulders/legs.
explanation: There are some things which a person can only do if there is someone more powerful helping him from above.

wolof: Kuy naan, di nëbbu, boo jangee, feeñ.
variants: Kuy naan di nëbbu, saa yu jangee feeñ.
Ku nëbbu di naan, boo màndee feeñ.
Nëbbu naan, màndi feeñ.
translation: The person who drinks (alcohol) in secret will be exposed when he reels and staggers.
explanation: Whatever you hide and do not abandon will be revealed with time.
scripture: “The man of integrity walks securely, but he who takes crooked paths will be found out.” (Proverbs 10:9 NIV)

wolof: Ku la jam, doo nàcc !
translation: You do not bleed if you are stabbed.
explanation: This is an insult against those who suffer a humiliation or insult and give in without reaction. Honour demands that one fights.

wolof: Nit bu ca jom jógee, dara desatu ca.
translation: A man who has lost his jom has nothing left.
explanation: [jom is a sense of honour which shows itself by the refusal to be shown up, by a constant effort to reach what is expected of one, or by the great sacrifices made in order to protect one's respectability. It is a dignity which will not accept being ridiculed.]

wolof: Man gan, man sa bopp la.
translation: Being hospitable means mastering oneself.

wolof: Teraanga du tuut.
translation: Hospitality is not insignificant.
scripture: “Offer hospitality to one another without grumbling.” (1 Peter 4:9 NIV)

wolof: Kër bukki xasaw na, waaye fa la bukki dëkk.
translation: The home of an hyena stinks but all the same that is where it lives.
explanation: One should learn to conform to one's status, regardless of its weakness or insufficiencies, without regard to the opinions of others. This proverb is often used when someone wants to prove that he is at home in his status, social circle or environment.

wolof: Bu ma jiitu ci sama mbojj.
translation: Do not precede me to my grain threshing.
explanation: Keep off my patch. Yatma announced to his parents that he would like to marry Astou. A family meeting was called to discuss the marriage. Khali the older brother of Yatma said that Astou is closely related, and also she did not seem to be very good at housework, therefore she would make a poor choice for a wife. Their father interprets that Khali is encroaching on his prerogatives, and calls him to order with “Bu ma jiitu ci sama mbojj”.

wolof: Bul yebu ci sama mbojj.
translation: Do not interfere with my business. Mind your own business.
transcriptionNotes: The source prints this English rendering in the notes font; its wording has been preserved.

wolof: Maa ngi ci sa simis bi/mbubb mi/létt bi.
translation: I am in your shirt, your gown etc.
explanation: A way of complimenting someone on their clothes, hair etc.

wolof: Meew mu wayul tuuru na.
translation: Milk which hasn't curdled has spilt.
explanation: A young person has died.

wolof: Ñaan gu daje ak amiin la.
translation: It is a prayer that encounters an amen.
explanation: An idiom expressing that things could not have turned out better. This proverb is used when something that one had expressed a desire for happens by itself.

wolof: Sama jaan wàcc na.
translation: I have completed my task.
transcriptionNotes: The source prints this English rendering in the notes font; its wording has been preserved.

wolof: Sàqami nga samab lanc.
translation: You have chewed my mouthful.
explanation: To say exactly what someone else was going to say or what they were thinking.
equivalents: “You have taken the words right out of my mouth.”

wolof: Suma i bët dañoo rembet.
translation: My eyes overflow.
explanation: My eyes cause me to covet (because they are full of all the good things that they see).

wolof: Sunuy sikkim lakkandoo nañu.
translation: Our beards were burnt together.
explanation: We are in the same embarrassing situation.

wolof: Ku xamul “buur saay na”, xam “buur dee na”.
variants: Ku xamul buur saay na, dees na ko wax buur dee na.
translation: He who does not understand “The king has passed away,” should be told “The king has died.”
explanation: Someone who cannot take a hint in polite language should be told plainly what is necessary. With some people you must call a spade a spade.

wolof: Ku xamul “suur naa” dangay téye ca loxo ba.
variants: Ku xamul suur naa, ñu téye sa loxo.
translation: You should hold back the hand of the person who does not understand, “I am full”.
explanation: When a person does not know how to limit himself, he needs to be restrained. [In Senegal, it is a mark of politeness for a host to encourage a guest to eat, and for a guest to limit what he eats with the excuse that he is full].
scripture: “When you sit to dine with a ruler, note well what is before you, and put a knife to your throat if you are given to gluttony.” (Proverbs 23:1-2 NIV)

wolof: Lu wagajaane maye du and ak njariñ.
translation: That which is obtained by illicit means will not bring any benefit.
scripture: “Such is the end of all who go after ill-gotten gain; it takes away the lives of those who get it.” (Proverbs 1:19 NIV)

wolof: Ku yàkkamti sa wërsëg, amiin wa ñaaw.
translation: Whoever is in too much of a hurry to receive his luck, the “amen” will be ugly.
explanation: The person who is in too much of a hurry to receive his luck will end up using dubious means and risk losing his reputation and his honour.

wolof: Yàkkamti ak gaawantu, bu ñu jurée doom, réccu am caw yoon.
variants: Yàkkamteek gaawtu bu ñu juree doom, réccu am caw yoon.
Yàkkamteek gaawantu, bu ñu juree doom, réccu am ca turandoo.
translation: Impatience and hurry, when they have a baby, always bring regrets.
transcriptionNotes: The source prints this English rendering in the notes font; its wording has been preserved.

wolof: Yàkkamti yàqule.
variants: Yàkkamti, yàqati.
translation: Be in a hurry; suffer ruin.
explanation: When you do things in a hurry you are likely to do things carelessly and make costly mistakes.

wolof: Yàkkamti, muj ga : yàqati.
translation: Hurry in the end brings ruin.

wolof: a. Merum ginaar lu muy wàññi tusuñe ?
variants: b. Merum ginaar saful tusuñe.
translation: a. How can the anger of a chicken harm the cook? b. The anger of the chicken does not disturb the cook.
explanation: At the market, Mary has set up her little stand. The local tax collector passes to receive her fee. She explains that she does not have anything to pay him as she has not yet sold anything, and asks him to pass by again later. He refuses, and the discussion gets heated. He insists that she pays immediately or he will call the police. To convince her of her impotence he cites this proverb.

wolof: Merum golo saful boroom tool.
translation: The anger of a monkey does not disturb the owner of the field.
explanation: At the market, Mary has set up her little stand. The local tax collector passes to receive her fee. She explains that she does not have anything to pay him as she has not yet sold anything, and asks him to pass by again later. He refuses, and the discussion gets heated. He insists that she pays immediately or he will call the police. To convince her of her impotence he cites this proverb.

wolof: Merum janax saful muus.
translation: The anger of a mouse does not disturb the cat.
explanation: At the market, Mary has set up her little stand. The local tax collector passes to receive her fee. She explains that she does not have anything to pay him as she has not yet sold anything, and asks him to pass by again later. He refuses, and the discussion gets heated. He insists that she pays immediately or he will call the police. To convince her of her impotence he cites this proverb.

wolof: Doxatu géléem, kow la jëm.
translation: The fart of a camel rises up.
explanation: One cannot prevent the evolution of something which will eventually be evident.

wolof: Ngësëm wacce wu ma dama ñor tabbi.
translation: It is not because you shook the tree that the fruit fell but rather because the fruit is ripe.
explanation: Everything happens in its time.

wolof: Bukki wiiri-wiiri, jaari Ndaari.
variants: Lu bukki wiiri wiiri, jaari ndaari.
translation: However much an hyena wanders about, he will eventually come to his den.
explanation: There are some things which a person will inevitably return to, things which he did habitually, even if planned to abandon them.

wolof: Ndoxum kese du forox.
translation: Pure water never turns sour.
explanation: Water does not alter itself. Any change is due to something foreign in the water. Likewise it is often due to the influence of others that people change their ideas. Souleyman and Omar decide to leave their village to go work in the city. They agree to keep it secret until their departure. However Omar’s family learns of their plans and prevents him from leaving. Omar accuses Souleman of having betrayed him. Souleyman defends himself saying he would never do anything like that. His uncle who has been listening to the argument interrupts with this proverb. A man has a sheep to sell, and comes to an agreement on the price with a buyer. When he gets home he tells his wife that he is selling the sheep for 7,000 cfa. His wife tells him that he is stupid because the sheep is worth at least 30,000 cfa. The next day when the buyer comes around to pick up his sheep, the seller announces that the price has changed. The buyer then quotes this proverb.

wolof: Lu waay nangu, teg ko ko dagan na.
variants: Lu nit nangu, teg ko ko dagan na.
translation: It is legitimate to place on someone any burden he is willing to accept.
explanation: An injustice becomes a justice the moment a person accepts to carry the burden. It is an encouragement to fight against injustice and not just accept it.

wolof: Ku reew, amul saans.
translation: The insolent and rude person has no sense.

wolof: Ku reew ñàkk lépp.
translation: The insolent lose everything.

wolof: Reewaande ga du jariñ mukk.
translation: Insolence is never of use.

wolof: Xale bu reew, toolam du ñor.
translation: The field of an insolent child does not ripen.

wolof: Ku xaste, waxeef nga loo doon.
translation: He who denigrates someone reveals who he really is himself.

wolof: Ku bañ ñu saaga la, doo saagaante.
translation: If you do not want people to insult you don't insult others.

wolof: Saaga ku la man duw fit ñàkk jom la.
translation: It is not courage that allows one to be insulting, it is a lack of honour.

wolof: Gàllaaj i nit mooy jub.
translation: The (best) amulet for a human being is honesty.

wolof: Ku sa bëgge bare, sa ngor néew.
translation: He who wants too much has little honour.
explanation: The Wolof belief that too much ambition is not good, and leads to a loss of honour.

wolof: Ku di loo xam wax ko, sa ngor yàqu.
translation: Whoever says all that he knows demeans himself.
scripture: A fool gives full vent to his anger, but a wise man keeps himself under control. (Proverbs 29:11 NIV) Wisdom reposes in the heart of the discerning and even among fools she lets herself be known. (Proverbs 14:33 NIV)

wolof: Ku di loo bëgg jaar ca, sa ngor yàqu.
translation: Whoever enters into everything that takes his fancy will demean himself (lose his honour and integrity).

wolof: Ku di foo yabu dem fa, sa ngor yàqu.
translation: Whoever goes wherever his fancy takes him will demean himself (lose his honour and integrity).

wolof: Néegub ngor, kenn terewu ko, ku ci duggul ci yow la.
translation: No one is forbidden from entering the room of honourable behaviour; if you do not enter it is your own fault.

wolof: Wéet duma tee gore.
translation: To be alone will not stop me from being honest.
explanation: Even when we are not accountable to anyone, it is good to be honest and manage well what has been entrusted to us.

wolof: Sorim réew bu m(u) la taxa fen.
translation: Being far from your country is not a reason to lie.

wolof: Du man rekk, bokkuma cee ko gën.
variants: Du man doŋŋ, bokkuma caa ko gën.
translation: “I was not part of it” is better than “I was not the only one”.
explanation: It is better not to be part of something dishonest than later on when you are caught to say that you were not the only one.
transcriptionNotes: A legacy PDF font maps the printed ŋ to õ in extracted text; ŋ has been restored after visual verification of the source glyph.

wolof: Ñaar a di yëf di jàmm ji àddina : ngor ak njullit.
variants: Ñaar di def jàmm ca àdduna : ngor ak njullit.
translation: Two things bring peace in the world: honourable behaviour (ngor) and piety (njullit).
transcriptionNotes: The source prints this English rendering in the notes font; its wording has been preserved.

wolof: Yebu ca, namm ca, ku la ca bëmëx nga jél.
variants: Namm ca, yabu ca, ku la ca bëmëx nga jël.
translation: So much the better to push someone to action who already wanted to do it.

wolof: Yebu ca, namm ca, ku la ca yónni, nga gaawa dem.
variants: Yebu ca nangu ca, ku la ca yónni nga gaaw ca dem.
translation: If you have made a decision to go to a place, and wish to go there, when someone sends you on an errand there you will be quick to go.
explanation: We go quickly where we are sent when we take interest in the journey.

wolof: Ñaar a di def aye ci àdduna : Njéemé ak Mbanik.
translation: There are two causes of disorder in the world: contrariness and intolerance.

wolof: Buur bu baax dina rafetal réewam.
translation: A good king will improve his kingdom.
scripture: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people. (Proverbs 14:34 NIV) Love and faithfulness keep a king safe; through love his throne is made secure. (Proverbs 20:28 NIV)

wolof: Buur bu baax dina sàmm i nitam.
translation: A good king will look after his subjects.

wolof: Buur aayul, dag yaa aay.
translation: The King is not evil, it is the courtiers who are evil.
explanation: With many of the things that you are deprived of by a ruler, it is the people close at hand to the ruler who deprive you, not the ruler himself. A self-seeking, servile flatterer and fawning parasite is dangerous.
scripture: The plans of the righteous are just, but the advice of the wicked is deceitful. (Proverbs 12:5 NIV) There is deceit in the hearts of those who plot evil, but joy for those who promote peace. (Proverbs 12:20 NIV)

wolof: Jege buur, jege xol baa ko gën.
translation: It is better to be close to the heart of the King than to be related to him.

wolof: Lu neex, Buur jël, ba mu des fuddu.
translation: The King can confiscate whatever he wishes except the pleasure of stretching oneself.
explanation: No matter what a ruler might decide there are things which he has no control over, and things which he cannot stop you doing.

wolof: Mere buur, jege xol baa ko gën.
translation: It is better to be close to the heart of the King than to be angry with him (which will serve no purpose).

wolof: Buur bu amul i nit du doon buur.
variants: Buur bu amul ay gaay, nguuram wóoral.
translation: A king without subjects is no king.
scripture: A large population is a king’s glory, but without subjects a prince is ruined. (Proverbs 14:28 NIV)

wolof: Buur du mbokk.
variants: Buur du mbokk, du jeneen.
translation: A king is not a relative.
explanation: A ruler should rule with impartiality and not give privileges to his relatives and friends. This proverb was one of a series of four sayings from a famous story from the life of Kocc Barma Fall, a sage from the 19th century, concerning his four pigtails.

wolof: Sopp buur aayul, wànte buur sopp laa ko gën.
variants: Sopp buur aayul, wànte buur bu la sopp a ko gën.
translation: It is not bad to love the King, but it is even better to be loved by the King.

wolof: Waxu buur waaw lay sant.
translation: The words of a king have the surname "Yes".
explanation: Mamoussé Diagne explains that there is always a risk in contradicting the words of a ruler or powerful person. His authority lies in his position, not his person. What he says is unimportant, and since he has power acquiescence is the wiser route to take.

wolof: Gàcce ak xamadi, laajul a ko indi.
translation: Failing to ask brings shame and ignorance.
scripture: You do not have, because you do not ask God. (James 4:2 NIV)

wolof: Laaj ay taxa xam.
translation: Questioning brings knowledge.
scripture: If any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him. (James 1:5 NIV)

wolof: Xam-xam sorewul, dafa làqu.
translation: Knowledge is not far away, it is simply hidden.

wolof: Bala ngaa xam, xamadi xaw laa rey.
variants: Bala ngaa xam, xamadi xaw laa gaañ.
Bala ngay xam, xamadi rey la.
Ku daa-ta xam xamadi xaw la rey.
translation: Before you know something, ignorance will almost have killed you.
explanation: It is through making many mistakes that one gains knowledge.

wolof: Du xamum nganj, yàgg a suub la.
variants: Du xam nganj, mës a suub la.
Du miin nganj, yàggal suub la.
Lii du xam nganj, mën suub la.
translation: It's not because you are familiar with indigo, but that you have been practising the art of dyeing for a long time.
explanation: Experience is much more important than knowledge.

wolof: “Xamul” aay na wànte “laajtewul” a ka yées.
variants: Xamul aay na, tey laajtewul a ko raw.
translation: It is bad enough to not know, but it is even worse to not ask.
explanation: Ignorance is bad enough but it is even worse not to inform yourself.
equivalents: “He who asks may be a fool for five minutes, but he who does not ask remains a fool forever.”

wolof: Xam-xam ñeent a koy kulóor : di ko bind, di ko jàngale, di ko waxtaane, mbaa di ko jëfe.
translation: There are four things to do with knowledge: write it, teach it, talk about it, and do it.
scripture: And the things you have heard me say in the presence of many witnesses entrust to reliable men who will also be qualified to teach others. (2 Timothy 2:2 NIV) Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. (Matthew 7:24 NIV)

wolof: Njiit du ki jiitu, ki nu jiital la.
translation: The true leader is not the person who is in front, but the person who is chosen to lead.
explanation: The fact of holding a position of responsibility is not a privilege in itself. The leader is called to serve the interests of those he leads. The good leader should make his decision conscious of the fact that he was chosen by others because of his qualities and availability. This is often used to put leaders who have become a bit full of themselves back in their place.

wolof: “Su doon man”, dey yàq mbooloo.
translation: “If it were me” destroys the group.
explanation: The braggart destroys the unity of a group. “Me! Me!” cries the braggart without worrying about others. Someone who wants to become the leader at all costs is not necessarily the person with the best virtues to be leader. The good leader is often the person who waits patiently for the group to recognise his qualities.

wolof: Mana, mana joo dégg, du moom.
translation: “It is me, it is me!” that you hear does not mean that that person has the necessary qualities.
explanation: The braggart destroys the unity of a group. “Me! Me!” cries the braggart without worrying about others. Someone who wants to become the leader at all costs is not necessarily the person with the best virtues to be leader. The good leader is often the person who waits patiently for the group to recognise his qualities.

wolof: Sàmm bu baax moo xam fa ñaxum noor di baree.
translation: A good shepherd knows where grass is plentiful during the dry season.
explanation: A good leader knows how to make arrangements for the benefit of his group.
scripture: I am the gate; whoever enters through me will be saved. He will come in and go out, and find pasture. (John 10:9 NIV) I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. (John 10:11 NIV) I am the good shepherd; I know my sheep and my sheep know me... (John 10:14 NIV)

wolof: Sikkim la, geestoo ko yóbbaale.
variants: Fu sikkim jëm, séen ko fa yóbbu.
translation: The chin goes with the head when it turns to look back.
explanation: One should take into account those who are affected by a decision before taking action.

wolof: Jàng du wees.
translation: It is never too late to learn/study.
equivalents: “You are never too old to learn.”

wolof: Ku jàngul du tari.
translation: If you have not studied, you will not recite (the Koran).
explanation: What you have not learnt you do not know well enough to be able to do.

wolof: Àddina daramba la.
explanation: Dab: To reach, Raw: To bypass, Ba: to abandon, to live. According to Maam Daour Wade this proverb is said to have been made up by the late Murid General Kalife Seex Abdul Ahad Mbàkke. Only the beginning of the words are used to form this proverb. Its meaning is that we come to life at some point in the world’s evolution. We have to struggle to live, and we will die at the end anyway.
transcriptionNotes: No separate literal English translation is supplied in the source; consult the explanation and any English equivalent.

wolof: Àddina gudd nab tank.
translation: Life can lead anywhere.
explanation: One has to think before doing anything because the consequences, good or bad, are waiting for him or her in the future.
scripture: I have seen something else under the sun: The race is not to the swift or the battle to the strong, nor does food come to the wise or wealth to the brilliant or favour to the learned; but time and chance happen to them all. (Ecclesiastes 9:11 NIV)

wolof: Àddina, kendandoo la.
translation: Life is like a day spent together.
explanation: Life does not last forever.

wolof: Àddina du kër, xaarukaayu dee la.
translation: The world is not a house; it is merely the waiting room of death.
explanation: We will all die and it can come anytime, therefore we should live with that fact in mind.
scripture: Show me, O LORD, my life’s end and the number of my days; let me know how fleeting is my life. (Psalms 39:4 NIV) Remember how fleeting is my life. For what futility you have created all men! (Psalms 89:47 NIV) Man born of woman is of few days and full of trouble. He springs up like a flower and withers away; like a fleeting shadow, he does not endure. (Job 14:1-2 NIV) for he knows how we are formed, he remembers that we are dust. As for man, his days are like grass, he flourishes like a flower of the field; the wind blows over it and it is gone, and its place remembers it no more. (Psalms 103:14-16 NIV) Man is like a breath; his days are like a fleeting shadow. (Psalms 144:4 NIV)

wolof: Àddina Njéeme la tudd, sant Ba.
translation: The first name of life in this world is “try” and its surname is “give it up”.
explanation: A person spends his life trying and always end up passing away.

wolof: Àddina këru naxekaay la.
translation: The world is not a real house.
explanation: Everything that we have in the world is temporary.
scripture: “For here we do not have an enduring city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.” (Hebrews 13:14 NIV)

wolof: Àddina njoowaanu golo la, garab gu nekk lay wékku.
translation: Life is like the swing of a monkey which he hangs on any tree.
explanation: The short duration and instability of life shows that life is not worth living if it were not possible to profit from life by meriting the gratitude of God and man through one’s good works.

wolof: Àddina potu ndaa la, ku naan jox sa moroom mu naan.
translation: Life is like the cup of a water jar; the one who has finished drinking passes the cup to another to drink.
explanation: We all die and pass on our heritage to others. The generations come and go. We all must give up our place to others. This proverb is often used at funerals.
scripture: I hated all the things I had toiled for under the sun, because I must leave them to the one who comes after me. (Ecclesiastes 2:18 NIV)

wolof: Àddina, reenub ñàmbi la, kenn xamul fu muy damme.
translation: Life's like a cassava root, no one can tell where exactly it will break.
explanation: Things happen without us being able to know sometimes when or how.
scripture: Why, you do not even know what will happen tomorrow. What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. (James 4:14 NIV)

wolof: Àddina, ñett a ci di yóbbal : ab xame, ab taar ak mbuus.
translation: Three things are necessary in this world: a friend, beauty, and money.

wolof: Àddina ñett a ci gën : àjjana biti, ak weerteewlu ak mëneek say dëkk, ak ku la gis bëgg la.
translation: Three things are important in life: good health, strength and harmony with one's neighbours; that is to say, to be loved by everyone.

wolof: a. Àddina ñett a ci gën, am a gën, man a gën, xam a gën.
variants: b. Xam a gën.
c. Man a gën.
translation: a. There are three things in life which are best: to have; to be able; and to know. b. Knowledge is best. c. Power is best.
explanation: Three things are desirable in this world: to increase one's wealth, one's power, and one's knowledge.

wolof: Àddina ñetti fan la, démb ñoom baay, tey ñun, ëllëg sunuy doom.
translation: Life consists of three days; yesterday was our father's, today is ours, and tomorrow is our children's.

wolof: Àddina jigéen la, ju fu mu tollu, mu ngi ëmb te kenn xamul lu muy jur.
translation: Life is like a woman who is constantly pregnant, and no one knows what she will give birth to.
explanation: No one can know what will happen during life.

wolof: Àddinaa ngi ci sunu kanam.
translation: Life is ahead of us.
explanation: What's going to happen is before us; meaning that we should not hurry, we will see what's going to happen.

wolof: Bëñ du ree jàmm !
translation: A tooth does not laugh at peace.
explanation: We sometimes laugh at human tragedies.

wolof: Bu ñii di jooy, ñee ngay ree.
translation: When these people are crying, others are laughing.
explanation: Joys and pains are the two sides of life.
scripture: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot... a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance... (Ecclesiastes 3:2,4 NIV)

wolof: a. Àddina weeru koor la ; feek jant sowul, juubu du wees.
variants: b. Dund gu jeexagul, weeru koor la : juubu weesoogu ca.
Koor gu jant sowagul, juubu weesoogu ca.
translation: a. Life is like the month of Ramadan; as long as the sun has not set, one will not cease to make mistakes. b. Life is like the month of Ramadan; as long as it is not finished, it is always possible to accidentally break the fast.
explanation: One should never be too sure of oneself, as it is all too easy to make mistakes.
equivalents: “Don’t count your chickens before they hatch.”
“There’s many a slip between the cup and the lip.”

wolof: Dund gu jeexagul, weeru koor la : juubu weesoogu ca.
translation: Life is like the month of Ramadan; as long as it is not finished, it is always possible to accidentally break the fast.
equivalents: “Don’t count your chickens before they hatch.”
“There’s many a slip between the cup and the lip.”

wolof: Liggéeyal àddina ja mu mel ni dootoo dee, liggéeyal allaaxira ja mu mel ni suba ngay dee.
translation: Work for the world as though you will never die, and work for the afterlife as though you will die tomorrow.
explanation: Use all means possible (including occult) to live this life, and use prayers & rituals of Islam for the next one.
scripture: “If we live, we live to the Lord; and if we die, we die to the Lord. So, whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.” (Romans 14:8 NIV)

wolof: Bakkan waruw dàll la : fa muy dagge doo ko yëg.
variants: Bakkan waru dàll la, buy dagg boroom du ko yëg.
translation: Life is like the strap of a sandal which breaks without warning.
explanation: Death comes without warning.

wolof: Àddina du cere, waaye dañu koy laalo.
variants: Àddina du cere waaye lu mat a laalo la.
Àddina du cere waaye dees na ko laalo.
translation: Life is not couscous but all the same one should add a binder to it.
explanation: Laalo is a vegetable powder made from the leaves of baobab trees which binds couscous to make it sticky and therefore easy to swallow. This proverb is a recommendation that one should know how to make life agreeable through humour, optimism, and leaving aside the drive to have one's own needs met. It is about learning to maintain friendly relationships in community.

wolof: Opp ju metti du taxa dee.
variants: Opp ju metti bokkul ak dee.
translation: A severe malady does not always kill.

wolof: Lëg mën naa daw, waaye àttanul teg.
translation: The hare can run but it is not capable of carrying a saddle.
explanation: Everyone has his limits. The people in a village decided to have a well dug. They put together all the money they had available which amounted to 640,000 cfa. As this was not sufficient, they appealed for help from a development NGO. A delegate from the the village visited a representative of the NGO with the sum that had been collected. He explained that all the villagers were poor, and in spite of their good will, they could not do more, quoting this proverb.

wolof: Ngaaxi tukkal, kenn du ko perngal mboccor.
translation: No one places the large bags of an adult male camel on the flanks of a baby camel.
explanation: Sylla received a letter from the court in Thies. He asked his youngest son to go and find his older brother so he could read the letter to him. Fari who is in primary school says “I know how to read”. His father replied, “Of course you know how to read, but this letter is much too difficult for you”, and he quotes this proverb.

wolof: Lu reen jan-jan, reen a nga ca suufam.
variants: Lu reen jan jan, reen a nga ca suuf.
translation: No matter how deep a root runs, there is another below it.
explanation: No matter how much a person knows or has, there are those who know more or have more.

wolof: Tool bu fi ñay ruuj, gëléem su koy ji, seet lay mana wey.
translation: If a camel sows a field in the area that an elephant has cleared, he should limit himself to what he is capable of completing.
explanation: To be successful a person should know himself, his possibilities and his limitations, and not make judgements based on the capacities of others.

wolof: Ngasum ñàmbi ku ñu cay yoori goj, daa weesu reen ya.
variants: Ngasum puloox ku ca wuti ay goj booba weesu nga reen ya.
translation: If you go to get a rope in order to dig up the manioc plants, that means that you have really gone past the roots.
explanation: He who restrains himself exactly where he should, will always be able to get out of whatever he gets into and no one will be able to fault him.

wolof: a. Ku sa mbootu jotul, doo rogganti.
variants: b. Ku woddu jotul, doo boot i gamb.
c. Kuy boot jotul, ngay dolliy gamb.
d. Ku say sër jotul doo boot i gamb.
translation: a. If your cloth for tying the baby onto your back is too short, you don't cover the baby with another wrap. b,c,d. If your wrap-around skirt is too short (to reach around your waist) you will not carry calabashes tied onto your back (like a baby).
explanation: If you have limited means don't spend them on a project that's beyond them. One should have a sense of one's limitations.
scripture: "Suppose one of you wants to build a tower. Will he not first sit down and estimate the cost to see if he has enough money to complete it? For if he lays the foundation and is not able to finish it, everyone who sees it will ridicule him, saying, ‘This fellow began to build and was not able to finish.’ "Or suppose a king is about to go to war against another king. Will he not first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand men to oppose the one coming against him with twenty thousand? If he is not able, he will send a delegation while the other is still a long way off and will ask for terms of peace." (Luke 14:28-32 NIV)

wolof: Bala nga tontu, jëkkala dégg.
translation: Before you reply, understand first.
scripture: He who answers before listening—that is his folly and his shame. (Proverbs 18:13 NIV)

wolof: Ku amul baay, na sab nopp doon sa baay.
translation: For the fatherless, his ear should be his father.
explanation: In the absence of a father, a child should listen and learn from the wisdom of his elders.

wolof: Lu dugg ci benn nopp génn ca bale.
translation: What goes in at one ear goes out the other.

wolof: Bopp bu nar a barkeel, nopp ya cay sax day dégg um ndigal.
variants: Bopp bu naree am jàmm, yàlla da cay saxal nopp yuy dégg.
Bopp bu am njeriñ, noppi moo ca sax.
translation: A head that is going to be successful has ears growing on it that listen to advice.
explanation: If you want to be successful, you should listen to advice.
scripture: For lack of guidance a nation falls, but many advisers make victory sure. (Proverbs 11:14 NIV) Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed. (Proverbs 15:22 NIV)

wolof: Abb delloo la sant.
translation: The name of “abb” is “reimburse”.
explanation: Whatever one borrows should be returned.

wolof: Àbb, delloo ca gën.
translation: It is better to return that which is borrowed than to borrow.

wolof: Bëgg naa la, maa la raw mënu koo fey.
translation: “I love you” is not repaid by “I love you more.”
explanation: It is not by saying “I love you more” that you can outdo the person who says first “I love you”.

wolof: Xédd, dug bëgg.
translation: Lust is not love.
explanation: “Love” based on lust is not real love.
scripture: Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs. Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres. (1 Corinthians 13:4-7 NIV)

wolof: Bëtub mbëggeel, jéll nab gàkk.
variants: Bëtu mbëggeel jéll na ab gàkk.
Bëti mbëggeel, jéll na gàkk.
translation: The eye of love passes over faults.
explanation: The person who loves you ignores your faults and accepts you as you are, warts and all.

wolof: Bëtu mbëggeel du gis melo.
variants: Bëtub mbëggeel du xool melo.
translation: The eye of love does not see appearances.
explanation: The eye of love does not take into account what you look like.

wolof: Wërsëg dina jóge ci njoñ.
translation: Opportunities can come from one's restraints.
explanation: One can learn good lessons by going through difficulties.
scripture: No discipline seems pleasant at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace for those who have been trained by it. (Hebrews 12:11 NIV)

wolof: Melax gaaw na, waaye yóbbuwul wërsëgu kàkkatar.
variants: Melax a gën a gaaw, waaye du yóbbu wërsëgu kàkkatar.
Gaaw taxul yelaana dunde wërsëgu kàkkatar.
translation: Lightning is certainly fast, but it does not take away the luck of a chameleon.
explanation: Adversity cannot stop the man who was born under a lucky star. Regardless of the things he might deprive us of, a thief cannot deprive us of our luck or prevent us from knowing other opportunities.

wolof: Tey yaw ëllëg sa moroom.
translation: Today you, tomorrow your neighbour.
explanation: Your happiness of today could leave you tomorrow for another. That is why it is important to share with your neighbour.

wolof: Yaa fi sësay taxa donn/falu.
translation: To be the last resort allows one to be elected.
explanation: When there are no alternatives one takes what one can, even if it be less than adequate.
equivalents: “In the kingdom of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.”

wolof: Dëkkub gumba patt a fay buur.
variants: Dëkkub gumba, patt a fay njiit.
translation: In the city of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.

wolof: Ku amul ndey, nàmp maam.
variants: Ku amul yaay, nàmp maam.
translation: He who has no mother suckles on the breast of his grandmother.
explanation: If one cannot have everything which one desires, one should make the best of one's circumstances, and be content with what one can have.
equivalents: “Half a loaf is better than no bread.”
“You have to cut your coat according to your cloth.”

wolof: Bukki su la bëggee yapp, da la naan yaa ngi may xeeñi seel.
translation: If the hyena wants to devour you, he will say to you that you smell to him like strips of dried meat.
explanation: When a person wants something from you (to his advantage and not yours), he will tell you things that support what he wants in order to manipulate you to do what he wants.
scripture: "It’s no good, it’s no good!" says the buyer; then off he goes and boasts about his purchase. (Proverbs 20:14 NIV)

wolof: Bey ci sa toolu sëriñ bu doon maye barke kon seeni doom a cay jiitu.
translation: If cultivating the field of a marabout could bring blessing then you would see his children there first.

wolof: Sëriñ du sàcc, dafa randal, ba ñu fàtte, mu jël.
translation: The marabout does not steal; he merely puts it aside until no one thinks of it any longer, then he takes it.

wolof: Bu naar sonnee wax i wolof.
translation: When a Maure has problems he speaks Wolof.
explanation: When it is necessary a Maure will speak in Wolof.

wolof: Lu Naar gis ci mbuusam, ba sànni ko, ku ko for it du am njeriñ.
translation: What the Mauritanian has seen in his bag, and has thrown away, whoever picks it up again, will have no benefit.
explanation: A comment on the perceived stinginess of Mauritanians.

wolof: Bala nga ne “naam”, ne fa.
variants: Bala nga wuyu nekk fa.
Bala nga naan naam, ne fa.
translation: Before you answer “yes”, you must be there.
explanation: To do something one has to have the means.

wolof: Saaku bu deful dara du taxaw.
variants: Saaku bu deful, du taxaw.
translation: An empty sack cannot stand upright.
explanation: One cannot put a lot of energy into a project without the means. Without a good material foundation any project is bound to fail.

wolof: Yërmande day wàññi doole.
translation: Mercy makes one weak.

wolof: Bu ñépp yemee, am ñu gedd seen cër.
variants: Bu ñépp yemee, am ñu gedd seen wall.
translation: If one divides equally between all, there will be those who refuse their share.
explanation: One cannot put on the same level the worker and the idle; those who are knowledgeable and those who are ignorant; the traitor and the hero. Justice demands that each receives according to his merit.

wolof: Kuy aaye xobu màngo, doo ca mayeeb doom.
translation: The person who does not permit you to touch the leaves of the mango tree will not give you its fruit.

wolof: Sakkantal du la taxa texe.
translation: Being miserly will not cause you to be saved.
scripture: One man gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds unduly, but comes to poverty. (Proverbs 11:24 NIV)

wolof: Dereti bopp du moy mbaggum boroom.
variants: Deretu bopp, du moy mbagg.
Deretu bopp, du moy mbagg moy baat.
translation: The blood which runs from the head will inevitably fall on the shoulders.
explanation: A misfortune which afflicts those close to us will also affect us.

wolof: Picc mu lakk taat a fi gëna bëgg moroom.
variants: Picc mu lakk bopp a gëna bëgg moroom.
translation: A bird with a burnt rump/head wants a fellow.
explanation: One does not like to be alone in misfortune.

wolof: Njuumte du ñàkk, yàgg caa bon.
translation: Mistakes will always happen. The bad thing is to persist in them.

wolof: Ku nekk ci xare warula ree ku ñu jam.
translation: Someone who is in a battle should not laugh at someone who has been stabbed.
explanation: One should not laugh at people in difficult situations as you never know when it might happen to you. The friends of a young pregnant girl make fun of her. An elderly woman overhears them and cites this proverb.
equivalents: “People who live in glass houses should not throw stones.”

wolof: Ku nekk ci biirub ndox, warula ree kuy lab.
translation: Someone who is in the water should not laugh at the person who is drowning.
explanation: One should not laugh at people in difficult situations as you never know when it might happen to you. The friends of a young pregnant girl make fun of her. An elderly woman overhears them and cites this proverb.
equivalents: “People who live in glass houses should not throw stones.”

wolof: Nebbon bi ci dënnu tuabéer, ba tax ko tëbëntu, mungi ci xàbban te mu ne tekk ak moom.
translation: The hump of animal fat which hangs from the chest of the ram, and incites it to manifest its power is also found on the steer, which however remains calm.
explanation: Modesty is something to be valued. When one boasts of something whether it be knowledge, strength or fortune, there is always someone else who has far more yet without feeling the need to boast or show up the vanity of others. [tulaabéer = race of sheep; xàbban = steer, (castrated bull)]
scripture: This is what the LORD says: "Let not the wise man boast of his wisdom or the strong man boast of his strength or the rich man boast of his riches, but let him who boasts boast about this: that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD, who exercises kindness, justice and righteousness on earth, for in these I delight," declares the LORD. (Jeremiah 9:23-24 NIV)

wolof: Leketug kese, naxul i béy.
variants: Leketu neen du naxu béy.
translation: An empty bowl will not trick a goat (into coming).
explanation: There are limits to naivety. One cannot let oneself be taken in by any old trap. If you want someone to do something for you then you need to show them that you are genuine, not just use talk.

wolof: Sant dëkkul fenn.
translation: The surname does not live anywhere.
explanation: The family name no longer allows one to know the origin (whether ethnic or geographical) of a person.

wolof: Bant, lu mu yàgg yàgg cig dex, du tax mu soppiku jasig.
variants: Yàggaayu bantu ron ci ndox, du ko tax a doon jasig.
Bant, lu mu yàgg, yàgg ci dex, du ko tax a soppaliku jasig.
translation: No matter how long a log soaks in the river, it will never become a crocodile.
explanation: One cannot change one's nature simply by imitation. This is often used in the context of changing culture. Learning Wolof language and culture will never be enough for a Westerner to become Wolof.

wolof: Aw doj du yàgg géej ba tax mu doon aw jën.
translation: A stone, no matter how long it spends in the ocean, will not become a fish.
explanation: One cannot change one's nature simply by imitation.

wolof: Golo ñaawul, baay ba la niru.
variants: Bukki ñaawul, baay ba la niru.
translation: The monkey is not ugly; it simply resembles its father.
explanation: One should render to nature that which belongs to nature.

wolof: Ku jél rongooñ, siim cereem, bu ko ñaan ñeex.
variants: Kuy jooy di bëse kenn du la ñaan am ñeex.
Kuy jooy di siime du maye am ñeex.
translation: Someone who wets the couscous with her tears should not be asked for sauce.
explanation: There is no point in asking something from someone who has nothing. Someone who cannot meet his own needs, cannot meet the needs of others. He who does not have sufficient for himself is unlikely to give to others.

wolof: Ku laaxul lekk, doo laax jaay.
variants: Ku laaxul lekk, laaxtil jaay.
Bala kenn di laax jaay, laax lekk.
translation: She who doesn't cook laax to eat, will not cook laax to sell.
explanation: Someone who is dying of starvation does not sell their food.

wolof: Bala ngaa xam luw taat di jëriñ, mbate toog jotee.
variants: Bala ngay xam li taat di jariñ, toog jot.
Bala ngaa xam lu taat di jëriñ mbee jékki jotee.
translation: One only knows the value of the backside when one has to sit down.
explanation: A man leaves his village to go and live in the city. He abandons all contact with those of his age until the day he finds himself in need, and returns to the village. One of his old mates quotes him this proverb.

wolof: Gor, bu ñàkkee, fàttaliku bor.
translation: When an honest man is in need, he remembers the debts that are owed to him.
explanation: When one is in need, one is forced to scrape the bottom of the barrel, and chase after all his outstanding debts.

wolof: Mar du ma tax a naan póotit.
variants: Mar du tax a naan am póotit.
Bu la mar tax a naan póotit.
translation: My thirst is not a reason why I will drink the waste water from washing.
explanation: Even if one has nothing one must not steal or do wrong. Difficulties of life are not an excuse for bad behaviour.
scripture: Better a poor man whose walk is blameless than a fool whose lips are perverse. (Proverbs 19:1 NIV) Better a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take warning. (Ecclesiastes 4:13 NIV)

wolof: Alalu ku sàggan, ku farlu moo koy jariñoo.
translation: The enthusiastic person will profit from the riches of the neglectful.

wolof: Dég-dég amul i tànk, waaye jàll nam ndox.
variants: Dég-dég amul i tànk, waaye dina jàll dex.
translation: News does not have feet but it will cross the river.
explanation: [nam = na am]

wolof: Namm reytil weer.
translation: Nostalgia does not kill the month.
explanation: Nostalgia will not change the march of time.

wolof: Tunguni du teew, ñu di ko nataal.
translation: There is no need to draw a picture of a dwarf (to depict what one is like), if one is standing before you.
explanation: Things which are obvious do not need to be explained.

wolof: Wutinu xasin aminu ñeewin.
translation: You are trying badly to get rich, while people gossip about you, but when you become rich, they will envy you.
explanation: Don't listen to those gossiping while you're doing your best to make it because they'll be the ones envying you once you succeed.

wolof: Daw, ca ba ngay am i tànk.
translation: Run while you still have legs.
explanation: To get up and go is better than waiting until it is too late.

wolof: Ku bañ céebo nangum xaar.
translation: He who turns his nose up at the first rains must wait.
explanation: The peasant who does not want to sow his field with the first rains must wait until the wet season is properly established. If you turn up your nose at the opportunity before you, you must have the patience to wait for another opportunity to present itself.
equivalents: “Never put off till tomorrow what you can do today.”

wolof: Béy wéy na mbuus.
variants: Béy wees na mbuus.
Béy bi ñu yàpp, wees na mbuus.
translation: The goat has passed the bag.
explanation: The goat which has been devoured (by wild animals) is already past the point of being turned into a bag. In skinning the carcass of a goat if a slit is made on the chest it can no longer be made into a water bag. The occasion to use it as a bag has therefore passed. This time it is already too late for what one wants to do.

wolof: Dund gu jeexagul, lu nekk xaj na ca.
variants: Dund gu jeexagul, guddi gu bët setagul la, lu ne xaj na ca.
Dund gu sotteegul, lu ne xaj na ca.
translation: While life has not yet finished all is still possible.
equivalents: “While there is life, there is hope.”

wolof: Baroom jur ci sa tool taxul nga yett giir.
variants: Ku baroom jur ci sa tool, taxti la yett engu.
translation: The fact that an antelope gave birth in your field is not a reason to carve a bowl for milking (because she will not stay there).
explanation: One cannot always profit from an occasion.

wolof: Ku xëy tëdd, dinga gontoo daw.
translation: The person who spends the morning in bed will spend the afternoon running around.
explanation: Good organisation is essential for success in work. It also has a wider sense that if one wastes one's youth, one will try and catch up as an adult often with pain. At the age of 56 Alassane is having lots of problems finding a suitable wife, whereas his peers have been married for years. His friend and counsellor, the old Farba, quotes this proverb to help him understand that it would have been much easier to find a wife if he had begun looking before a certain age.

wolof: Gan doxat la balaay reyee, dem.
translation: A guest who farts, before it kills anyone, he will be gone.
explanation: Things which disturb you will not last for a long time.

wolof: Ku muñ, muuñ.
translation: He who is patient will smile.
explanation: All good things come to those who wait.

wolof: Ku yàgg cib teen, baag fekk la fa.
translation: The person who waits long enough at the well will eventually find a bucket to draw water with.
equivalents: “All things come to those who wait.”
“Good things come to those who wait.”

wolof: Lu waay muñ mu jeex.
translation: What a person patiently endures will come to an end.

wolof: Ndànk-ndànk mooy jàpp golo cib ñaay.
translation: Little by little, one catches the monkey in the forest.
explanation: It is with little steps than one can achieve the big tasks.

wolof: Koo ne duma la topp fa ngeen jëm dafa sorewul.
variants: Boo nee nit duma ko topp, booba fa ngeen jëm soriwul.
translation: If you say to someone, “I will not follow up on you”, then where you are going together is not far away.
explanation: Patience has its limits. If you allow someone to do as they see fit it is only because you do not have to tolerate it for long.

wolof: Yoonu jàmm du wiir.
translation: The way of peace is never winding.
explanation: The solution which solves the crisis and brings peace is usually the most simple. Peace is worth everything.

wolof: Jàmm, ca la ñépp xaj.
variants: Jàmm ci la lépp xaj.
translation: Everything is contained in peace.
explanation: Peace is the (only recipient) that all men can enter into and be at ease.

wolof: Bakkan, jàmm la bëgg.
variants: Bàkkan, jàmm lay laaj.
translation: The soul aspires only to peace.
explanation: This proverb demonstrates the importance of peace in Wolof culture.

wolof: Nawle, nit rekk ka ko sonnal.
translation: There is no one that causes so much trouble as a peer.
explanation: David Maranz explains that this is understood to mean that the competition of the nawle forces a person to make uncomfortable or inconvenient efforts so as to not be left in an inferior position or fall behind in any way.

wolof: Nit ku nekk àddina war na bàyyi xel nawleem.
translation: Everyone in this world had better pay attention to his or her peer.
equivalents: This mind-set results in extraordinary efforts to keep up with peers (“to keep up with the Joneses”) in dress, possessions, gift giving etc.

wolof: Lu picc bare, bare, du teree ji dugub.
translation: No matter how many birds there are, that will not prevent the sowing of millet.
explanation: Do not give up your project on the pretext of difficulties.

wolof: Saan su baree, dal.
translation: Throw many pebbles, and one will end up reaching the target.
equivalents: “If at first you don't succeed try, try and try again.”

wolof: Njort lu ñaaw dinay faral di wattu boroom.
translation: Pessimism can guard its owner.
explanation: Pessimism and mistrust can prove to be beneficial. It can be useful to take into account the negative aspects of a situation in order to neutralise them.

wolof: Tabaski du bés bu nekk.
translation: Tabaski is not celebrated every day.
explanation: One cannot have pleasure all the time. Not every day is a special occasion. Life consists both of moments of joy as well as pain. This proverb is often used by fathers on the days when they do not bring home any treats, and the children complain. Tabaski, when Muslims remember Abraham sacrificing his son, is the most important annual celebration in Senegal, of similar importance to Christmas in the West.

wolof: Du bés bu nekk baay rey gaynde.
translation: It is not every day that father kills a lion.
explanation: One cannot have pleasure all the time. Not every day is a special occasion. This proverbial expression is generally used lightly with amusement.

wolof: Du bés bu ne baay ray nag.
translation: It is not every day that father kills a cow.
explanation: One cannot have pleasure all the time. Not every day is a special occasion. This proverbial expression is generally used lightly with amusement.

wolof: Du bés bu set baay rey mbëtt.
translation: It is not every day that father kills a monitor lizard.
explanation: One cannot have pleasure all the time. Not every day is a special occasion. This proverbial expression is generally used lightly with amusement.

wolof: Ku yaru, falu.
translation: The person who is polite will be elected.
explanation: Politeness brings respect.

wolof: Sukk du tee yóbbu say wóom.
translation: Kneeling will not prevent you leaving with your knees.
explanation: Humility and politeness do not take anything away from anyone. So you have nothing to lose from being polite, and showing your respect for the other person. The proverb refers to the African traditional etiquette of genuflection or curtsy as a sign of respect.

wolof: Baadoolo dafay yemale bëgg-bëggam.
translation: The poor must limit his desires.

wolof: Kuy reere pann, boo woppee fande.
translation: Whoever eats the leftovers from the night before for dinner, when you are sick you will go hungry that night.
explanation: If you means are limited when you are well, things will be even worse when you are sick.

wolof: Baadoolo bu ragal naaj ragal na njariñam.
variants: Baadoolo bu bañee naaj, bañ nak mbokkam.
translation: A peasant who fears the sun fears what is useful to himself.
explanation: A peasant who refuses to work under the sun, distances himself from the only means of escaping his poverty.
scripture: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest— and poverty will come on you like a bandit and scarcity like an armed man. (Proverbs 6:10-11 NIV) Lazy hands make a man poor, but diligent hands bring wealth. (Proverbs 10:4 NIV) He who loves pleasure will become poor; whoever loves wine and oil will never be rich. (Proverbs 21:17 NIV) He who gathers crops in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son. (Proverbs 10:5 NIV)

wolof: Ku xarfa fuufawul, fuufa xarfa la.
translation: He who fails to prepare, prepares to fail. [xarfa and fuufa have no meaning in Wolof.]

wolof: Lu ni këtt, lu ne jonn a koy faj.
translation: The unexpected can only be solved by what is on hand and available.
explanation: If you want to solve unexpected problems, you need to put something aside in advance.

wolof: “Jàppal, ma yenni la”, du sawar laa yenni, waaye bëgga xam la nga yenu la.
variants: Am na ku la ne “ma yen la” ; booba, la ca ndab la la bëgga gis.
Am na ku la ne ma yen la, tey sa ndab la bëgg séet.
translation: “Hold on, let me help you put down the load on your head” does not come from a desire to help but rather to see what you are carrying.
explanation: When some offer their services to help you with what you are carrying on your head, they are only motivated to see what you are carrying.

wolof: Aar moo gën faj.
translation: Protection is better than treatment or cure.

wolof: Mag, day fàggandiku.
translation: The wise will take precautions.

wolof: Ñag, bala ngay ruurle.
translation: Enclose your field before the herds get in and devastate it.
equivalents: “An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.”

wolof: Fegoo gën faju.
variants: Fàggoo gën faju.
Fàggandiku moo gën a faju.
Fagaru moo gën faju.
explanation: It is better to stop bad things from happening than trying to solve problems afterwards.
transcriptionNotes: No separate literal English translation is supplied in the source; consult the explanation and any English equivalent.

wolof: Nég ba jaan dem, nga topp ca watit way dóor.
variants: Xaar ba jaan dem nga topp ca watit way dóor.
Bàyyi nga jaan dóor watit wa.
Bàyyi ba jaan wéy, nga topp ca watit wa di dóor.
Bul bàyyi jaan ba mu dem, nga topp ca watit way dóor.
Bul xaar ba jaan wéy ngay dóor ci watit wa.
translation: Wait until the snake has left then strike his track.
explanation: Two friends, Awa and Ndey go to a jeweller. Ndey orders a piece of jewellery and pays a deposit. Two weeks later she returns to collect her jewellery, and the jeweller tells her he has no more gold and refuses to return her deposit. She tells Awa of her misadventure who says to her that she thought he looked dishonest and she should not have paid a deposit. Ndey exclaims “You could have told me earlier” and quotes this proverb.
equivalents: “It's too late to shut the stable door after the horse has bolted.”

wolof: Xoddiku bala ngay lakkle.
variants: Xoddilu, ca ba nga lakkleegul.
translation: Clear the dry grass to prevent a fire before there is something burning.

wolof: Ku réy-réylu gaawa rus.
translation: The proud are quickly put to shame.

wolof: Réy day sewloo nit.
translation: Pride makes a man small.
scripture: When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with humility comes wisdom. (Proverbs 11:2 NIV) Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is found in those who take advice. (Proverbs 13:10 NIV)

wolof: Keppaarug ngunu jombul séq.
translation: The shade of the chicken house does not exceed the merit of the rooster.
explanation: Such a privilege is completely natural to such a person. A man had four wives who were not born in the same place, not brought up in the same manner, and did not behave in the same way towards him. To the wife who gave him the most respect, and held him in the highest regard, he gave the most happiness, and gave her secret favours which came from his heart. To the others who exasperated him, who did not follow his instructions he did not give the same favours. The other wives complained and he replied with this proverb.

wolof: Soppiw doxin jàllulum tan.
translation: Changing the way you walk, isn't of any help when it comes to crossing vast salinated lands.
explanation: One should not be making mistakes when choosing the means in solving problem cases.

wolof: Fii, wund du fi naane ñeex.
translation: Here the cat does not lap the sauce.
explanation: Opportunists have no chance here. Ami likes to take advantage of others. She often borrows things or clothes which she forgets to return. And when she does the shopping for others, the prices on that day are always exceptionally high. One day she visits Faya and asks to borrow her good boubou. Faya who knows what she is like, refuses and quotes this proverb.

wolof: Weddi, gis bokku ca.
translation: One cannot deny what one has seen for oneself.

wolof: Werante xuuxaan, tekki tubéy.
translation: Rather than arguing about a scrotal hernia, one should undo the pants.
explanation: Showing the proof puts an end to controversies.

wolof: Weddi, boo gisee, gëm.
variants: Weddil, soo gisee gëmal.
translation: Deny if you like, but when you see, believe.

wolof: Caga, benn yoon la ñu koy nax.
variants: Caga, kenn du ka nax ñaari yoon.
translation: No one deceives a prostitute twice.
explanation: In your relations with people if you deceive them once you will find them closed to you in the future.

wolof: Ku làqu ci ku ñu rus dinga raw.
translation: He who hides behind someone whom people are ashamed to attack will escape.
explanation: To attack a lizard on a water pot risks either breaking the pot or contaminating the water. It is at times strategic to count on protectors when in difficult situations. The cover of a person of influence or respect can sometimes be beneficial.

wolof: Sindax, ndaa lañu koy ruse.
translation: If the lizard is safe from attack it is because of the water pot he is sitting on.
explanation: To attack a lizard on a water pot risks either breaking the pot or contaminating the water. It is at times strategic to count on protectors when in difficult situations. The cover of a person of influence or respect can sometimes be beneficial.

wolof: Soo bëgg loo lekk nawet na nga di sakkantal ci noor.
