translation: If want to have something to eat during the wet season, then you need to be frugal during the dry season.
scripture: Ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in the summer. (Proverbs 30:25 NIV) Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise! It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest. (Proverbs 6:6-8 NIV)

wolof: Li béy doon dunde ba sax sikkim mën ca wéy ba dee.
variants: Lu bëy daan dunde ba sax sikkim, man na kaa dunde ba, xëy dee.
translation: The food which has sustained the billy goat to the point where it sprouts its beard is sufficient to continue to sustain it until death.
explanation: One should be careful about despising the work that has sustained one until now by entering into something else which might be worse.

wolof: Tooñ du gàllaaj.
translation: Provocation is not a protection.

wolof: Dendaale bu doon jariñ, dugub, xob yaa koy laalo.
variants: Su dendale doon jariñ, dugub, xob yaa koy laalo.
translation: If proximity was sufficient to be of use to something, then the millet would use its own leaves to thicken the couscous.
explanation: People or things that are close are not always in your proper interest. [Laalo is a vegetable powder made from the leaves of baobab trees which binds couscous to make it sticky and therefore easy to swallow.] Adam and Mary were born and grew up next door to each other. They love each other and want to marry. However Adam belongs to a caste. Adam’s parents think that the good situation of their son will break down the customary social barriers. So they send a delegation to Mary’s parents to ask for her hand in marriage. The delegation reminds them of their long-standing friendship, and close proximity as neighbours, and of the fact that the couple have known each other since childhood, so it would be best to allow them to marry. However Mary’s father responds brutally with this proverb.
transcriptionNotes: The source prints this English rendering in the notes font; its wording has been preserved.

wolof: Béy du raas déemi guddi.
translation: The goat does not glean jujubes (red dates) at night.
explanation: One should not head off for adventures.

wolof: Bul mere ka la yakkal ci gaalu xaj, boo ca lekkul mu jar ko.
translation: Do not be angry with the person who serves you a dog's bowl. It is sufficient to refuse to touch it.

wolof: Def loo man, wax loo xam, boo tëddee nelaw.
translation: Do only what you are capable of, speak only of what you know, and you will sleep soundly when you go to bed.
explanation: If one is content to live within one's means, and only speak of what one knows for sure, one will live in peace and happiness.

wolof: Gumba tal na leneen lu dul tëb i teen.
variants: Gumba tal na lu dul tëb i kàmb.
Gumbaa ngaak yitte yu dul tëb i teen.
translation: A blind man has other things to do apart from jumping around a well.
explanation: Prudence before certain acts to be accomplished is all the more important when the smallest mistake can lead to a catastrophe.

wolof: Jaan du tuut, saayu mattee boom.
translation: The smallness of a snake does not prevent its bite being fatal.
explanation: One must never minimise a danger.

wolof: Kenn du wax lu mu xamul.
translation: No one should say that which he knows not.

wolof: Nëbbul te ne gisuma kenn, waaye bul wax ne kenn gisu ma.
translation: Hide yourself and say, “I do not see anyone”, but don't say, “No one can see me”.
explanation: As well as you might hide your actions from others, the eye of society is watching through cracks that you do not suspect. And your actions will become known and commented on.

wolof: Kenn du toog ci bànqaas di ko gor.
translation: No one cuts the branch on which he is sitting.
equivalents: “Don't cut your nose off to spite your face.”

wolof: Kenn du boole say nen yépp ci genn leket.
translation: No one puts all his eggs in the same calabash.
equivalents: “Do not put all your eggs in one basket.”

wolof: Ku sol tubéyu nékk du jaaru.
translation: The person who wears pants of animal fat will not need to warm himself up.
explanation: In certain situations, one does not take risks.

wolof: Ni ñuy def saa njëkk kenn du ko def saa béjjén.
translation: That which one dares to do to a sheep without horns, one would never think of doing to a ram with horns.

wolof: Bëréb bukkeek mbaam yàgg-yàgg mbaam ay dee.
variants: Bëréb bukkeek mbaam.
translation: In a wrestling match between an hyena and a donkey, eventually the donkey will die.
explanation: The weak will always be overcome by the strong, so they should not fight with them.

wolof: Bët du gis la koy fatt.
variants: Bët, la koy fatt, du ko gis.
translation: Something which gets into the eye, the eye cannot see.
explanation: The things that you do sometimes come back at you with consequences that you do not expect. Therefore you should be careful in all that you do.
scripture: But if you fail to do this, you will be sinning against the LORD; and you may be sure that your sin will find you out. (Numbers 32:23 NIV)

wolof: Làmbi bukki, béy du ca wàlli.
variants: Béy du wàlli ci sabarug bukki.
translation: The place where the hyenas put on a wrestling match is not an event for a goat to attend.
explanation: Lamin is travelling far from home. Someone offers him a place to stay and tells him how to get there. But Lamin gets lost and asks an old man the way. The man is surprised that Lamin has the intention of passing the night there as the family has the reputation of being sorcerers. To try and persuade Lamin not to go there he cites this proverb. Rama is very proud to have received her first pay check. On her way home she stops to window-shop. Now being late she takes a shortcut along an infamous street where someone snatches her bag. She arrives home crying and tells her father the story. He cites this proverb.

wolof: Boroom caq war nay moytu boroom baatub neen.
variants: Boroom caq day moytu boroom yoqeel.
translation: The owner of a necklace should beware of him who has a bare neck.
explanation: One should be wary of one's company, especially the person in need.

wolof: Suuxlu mbër, làng ak moom a ko gën, muy bëre di daan ngay ree.
translation: It is better to be on the same side as a champion than against him. If you are on his side you can rejoice in his victories.
equivalents: “Discretion is the better part of valour.”

wolof: Duma jënd jaan ci pax.
variants: Duma jënd jaanum pax.
Duma jënd jaar ci pax.
Duma jënd janaxi pax.
translation: I will not buy a snake / ground squirrel / rat in a hole.
explanation: I won't buy what I have not seen. Show me first before I buy.
equivalents: “Never buy a pig in a poke.”

wolof: Daw ba rëcc, ci ngóora la bokk.
variants: Daw ba raw, ci ngóora la bokk.
translation: To succeed in escaping by running away as fast as one can is also part of heroism.
explanation: It is wise to avoid needless rashness which could expose you to unnecessary danger.
equivalents: “He who fights and runs away, may live to fight another day.”
“Discretion is the better part of valour.”

wolof: Kooyi bukki du njoowaanug tef.
variants: Kooyu bukki du njoowaanug tef.
translation: The penis of an hyena is not a swing for a kid (baby goat).
explanation: No matter how bold one is, one must know how to measure the recklessness of certain actions. When the mother of John explained that John was more turbulent at home than at school due to the severity of his teacher, she used this proverb. An old man known for his harshness had a mango orchard behind the village. After school the kids headed to the orchard to pinch the fruit. One day, the grandfather of one of the students surprised his grandson in the orchard and in warning cited this proverb.
equivalents: “Fools rush in where angels fear to tread.”

wolof: Ku ndóbin rey sa maam, foo séenati lu ñuul, daw.
variants: Ku ndóbin rey sa maam, foo séene lu ñuul war a daw.
Ku ndobin rey sa maam boo séenée lu ñuul daw.
Ku ndóbin ray sa maam, boo gisee lu ñuul wara daw.
translation: If a ground hornbill killed your grandfather, when you see something black you will flee.

wolof: Kuy jaay tamaate doo bëre : boo ca dëggee mu toj.
variants: Kuy jaay kamaate doo bëre : boo ca dëggee mu toj.
translation: Someone who sells tomatoes should not wrestle as he risks squashing his tomatoes by stepping on them.
explanation: If you do not have a firm hold on what you have, you should be careful about doing anything which could risk what you have. One should always be honest. A certain man starts a business which is at first successful. He begins to live above his means, going out on the town each night with friends having had homes in desirable locations for a long while. His cousin seeing what he is doing advises him that all his actions should bring wealth not consume it, and he cites this proverb.

wolof: Mag, lu dal xelam a koy may yaram.
variants: Mag, lay dalum xelam, moo koy may yaram.
translation: It is only that which brings peace of mind which can permit him to put on weight.
explanation: Only that which inspires inner confidence will permit a person to develop personally. Take sufficient precautions and not make commitments beyond one's capabilities in order to live without too much worry, but rather with a tranquil and calm spirit.
scripture: A man’s spirit sustains him in sickness, but a crushed spirit who can bear? (Proverbs 18:14 NIV)

wolof: Su ñu la séddee ci gaalu xaj itam, nanga fexe ba bu ca lekk.
variants: Mën nañu la yekkal ci gaalu xaj, waaye bu ca lekk.
Su ñu la yakkalee ci gaalu xaj, fexeel ba bu ca lekk.
Ku la sédd ci gaalu xaj, bu mu fekk nga cay lekk.
translation: If they serve you a dog's bowl, make sure you do not eat from it.
explanation: People can credit you with a bad reputation but don't act in a way that proves them right. Do not give he who denigrates you an opportunity to make fun of you. It is often used when one wants to put someone on guard against traps put out by his detractors.
scripture: Proud men have hidden a snare for me; they have spread out the cords of their net and have set traps for me along my path. Selah (Psalms 140:5 NIV) Free me from the trap that is set for me, for you are my refuge. (Psalms 31:4 NIV)

wolof: Ñu yemul i lor, duñu mëqandoo sunguf.
variants: Mëqandoo sunguf koo yemal i lor.
translation: Those who do not have the same amount of saliva do not compete to eat flour.
explanation: To face a rival it is best to have the same advantages as he. In life it is always essential to know one's capabilities and one's limits before starting something. Anta is a young school girl who would like to participate in a holiday program organised by her school. The program costs 9,000 cfa and all her companions have already registered and paid the fee. She begs her mother to give her the money. Her mother replies with this proverb to remind her of their modest situation. Mawa is a poor farmer. In spite of his meagre earnings, he invites all of his village and half of the next village to a celebration of the birth of his latest child. To pay for this he borrowed more than he could ever repay on time. He goes to find his principal creditor to ask him to be patient. The man rebukes Mawa for imitating those who are richer than he, quoting this proverb.
equivalents: “Cut your cloth according to your coat.”

wolof: Raay gaynde, dee fa yomb na.
variants: Raay gaynde dee fa, ku nekk mën na ko.
translation: To stroke a lion and die there is easy.
explanation: It is easy to get into something that is beyond you. To get out of it again with honour is difficult.

wolof: Wànnent ku mu bàyyi say bët nga bàyyiy bëtam.
variants: Wànneent ku mu bàyyi say get nga wara bàyyi yosam.
translation: If conjunctivitis leaves your eyes intact, you should leave its eyes alone as well.
explanation: If someone stronger than you leaves you alone, you should leave him alone. Don't disrupt a situation that is going well as it will only lead to problems.
equivalents: “Don’t beard a lion in his den.”

wolof: Xalu ndéef gëmm na, waaye feyul.
variants: Xalu ndéef gëmm na, ne feyul.
translation: The embers of cow dung are covered by ash but they do not go out.
explanation: A fire hides its embers below a layer of ash waiting for the unsuspecting to put in their hand. In other words appearances can be deceptive, so care is necessary in every situation.
equivalents: “Don't think still water has no crocodiles.”

wolof: Bañ loo mënula wàññi dara, mook bëgg yem.
translation: To refuse what you cannot stop is the same as agreeing.

wolof: Bëgg ju sañul feeñe, mook bañaale yem.
translation: A desire which one cannot manifest is the same as rejection.

wolof: Ku bañ lu baax, lu bon nga bëgg.
translation: Whoever rejects the good wants evil.

wolof: Bala kenn mën a làq ñeme li lay dàq.
translation: Before someone can protect you, he must have the courage to face that which is chasing you.

wolof: Bala ngay wut alal, na nga wut nit ñi.
translation: Seek friendship above wealth.
explanation: Human relations are far more precious than worldly wealth.

wolof: Boo yëkkëtee ab loxo ne yëguma kenn, yëkkëtil beneen bi ne kenn yëgu ma.
translation: When you raise your hand and it says “I respect no one”, the other will say “No one respects me.”
explanation: When someone doesn't give a damn about anyone, he should know that in principle, no one gives a damn about him.

wolof: Bul def jaambur loo beggul mu def la ko.
translation: Do not do to your neighbour what you do not want him to do to you.
scripture: Do to others as you would have them do to you. (Luke 6:31 NIV)

wolof: Cuuj, su woomalee, beru.
translation: Once a chick has found something to eat, it goes off on its own.
explanation: Alfa, an older distinguished man, is often called to the office of the regional administrator, who sometimes even asks him to accompany him on his trips throughout the region, because Alfa knows many people and speaks several local languages. In the village, his friends note that since he has become a VIP, they hardly ever see him at the village meeting place in the evenings. One of them jokes saying they are not longer good enough for him. Another goes one up on this by quoting this proverb.

wolof: Duma bëgg lu la neex ba ne la Yàllaa ngi lay nuyu.
translation: I do not want to please you to the point of telling you that God greets you.
explanation: As much as we might desire to please someone, there are limits which one cannot cross.

wolof: Ku la tooñ, bul feyyu.
translation: Do not repay him who does you harm.
scripture: Do not say, "I’ll pay you back for this wrong!" Wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you. (Proverbs 20:22 NIV) "You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth.’ But I tell you, Do not resist an evil person. If someone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if someone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. If someone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. (Matthew 5:38-41 NIV) Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse... Do not repay anyone evil for evil. Be careful to do what is right in the eyes of everybody. If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone. Do not take revenge, my friends, but leave room for God’s wrath, for it is written: "It is mine to avenge; I will repay," says the Lord. On the contrary: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals on his head." Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. (Romans 12:14, 17-21 NIV)

wolof: Ku bëgg ku la duma, tooñal ku la mën.
translation: If you want to be beaten up, then offend someone who is stronger than you.

wolof: Ku am nit ñi, ñàkkoo dara. Ku ñàkk nit ñi, amoo dara.
translation: Whoever has friends lacks nothing. Whoever does not have friends does not have anything.
explanation: It is through relationships with others that our needs are met and our potential is able to develop.

wolof: Lépp a ngi ci nit ñi.
translation: Everything is with people.
explanation: You should have as many friends as you can in order to be able to solve any problem you'll have in the future.

wolof: Lu waay ñàkk, waayam a ko amul.
translation: If an individual lacks something, it is because his friend does not have it.
explanation: Friends share their belongings. Between two friends, if one of them is missing something, it is because the other doesn't have it either.
scripture: A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity. (Proverbs 17:17 NIV)

wolof: Néew, bu rombeey armeel, robam dootul neex.
translation: The burial of a corpse, once it has bypassed the cemetery, will no longer be easy.
explanation: An uncle asks his nephew to give him a bag of rice. The nephew told him that he could not. A little while later the nephew loaned money to a neighbour. The uncle learnt of this, and being very unhappy he went to find his nephew and told him this proverb.

wolof: Su àndub ñaar yàggee, kenn a muñ.
translation: If two people manage to keep company for a long time, it is certain that one of them has been patient.
explanation: It is patience and tolerance which permits long term relationships.

wolof: Nit, nit ay garabam.
translation: The best medicine for a person is another person.
explanation: People are important…you can't solve everything yourself. The most precious treasure on earth is not riches but relations with other people. In Senegal the number of relatives, friends and neighbours who attend events such as naming ceremonies, weddings, funerals etc demonstrates the respect that one has. A well off man who prepares a feast with great pomp and finds himself alone with his food will understand that he should have paid more attention to developing relationships.

wolof: Ku amul i mbokk, amuloo dara, doo dara.
translation: He who has no relations has nothing and is nothing.
explanation: Mbokk in this proverb is in the broader sense of the word and includes relations of all sorts, blood or otherwise. The Wolof place a high value on relationships. The more relationships a person has, the great his importance and respectability.

wolof: Ña bokk lël, def ñu di ànd ba moos.
translation: Those who shared the same circumcision group become friends for life.

wolof: Ñu bokk teen ñooy laxasooy goj.
translation: It is those who share the same well who tangle their ropes.
explanation: The houses of Moussa and Badara are adjoining. The two families — especially the children — are always fighting with much noise, shouts and arguing. Their closest neighbour one day asks Moussa the cause of their frequent fights. Moussa smiles and quotes this proverb.

wolof: Bala ngaa toj gémmiñu sàmm dangay xam la mu waliis.
variants: Bala ngay fél gémmiñu sàmm, nga xam lu mu waliis.
Bul fél gémmiñug sàmm te xamoo la muy waliis.
Balaa ngaa toj gémmiñu sàmm, xaaral ba xam la mu waliis.
Balaa ngaa pes gëmmiñu sàmm xam lu mu waliis.
Bala ngaa mbej Samba, xamal la muy waliis.
Bala ngaa toj gémmiñu sàmm, na nga xam lu mu waliis.
translation: Before you slap the shepherd on the mouth, you should find out what he is whistling.
explanation: Do not be rash in judging people. You should avoid accusing people before listening to their side of the story, or you are likely to be mistaken in your judgement.

wolof: Dëmm rey la, jaale la.
variants: Dëmm rey la ba noppi jaale la.
translation: The vampire kills you and then comes to pay his condolences.
explanation: Someone can do you harm (behind your back), then come and sympathise with you (in hypocrisy).

wolof: Fakk naa laa gën a masuma laa gis.
variants: Fakk na la, moo gën xamuma la.
translation: 'I have forgotten your name' is better than 'I have never seen you before'.

wolof: Bëñ ak làmmiñ ñoo dëkk, bés bu set dañuy xuloo, waaye dañuy jubóowaat.
variants: Làmmiñ ak bëñ a dëkk.
translation: Teeth and tongue live together.
explanation: People living closely can quarrel but in the end they have to make peace.

wolof: Réeroo amul, ñàkk a waxtaan a am.
variants: Mbañ amul, ñàkk waxtaan a am.
Ñàkk a juboo amul, ñàkk waxtaan a am.
Ñàkk déggoo amul, ñàkk waxtaan a am.
translation: There is no such thing as a misunderstanding; there has simply been a lack of discussion.
explanation: Misunderstandings occur when people do not talk.

wolof: Mbaxana moo teg sa bopp jekku ca, bul ko teg ci boppu keneen.
variants: Mbaxana moo natt ci sa bopp, jekku ca, bu ko natt ci sa boppu nawle.
translation: If you do not consider that the hat on your head is appropriate, do not place it on the head of another.
explanation: Do not confer on someone else what you consider to be bad for yourself.

wolof: Paaka bi lay rendi, sa waay a koy daas, jox la.
variants: Paaka bi lay rey, say mbokk a koy daas.
translation: The knife which slits your throat was sharpened by your friend, and given to you.
explanation: Your best friend could be the instigator of your misfortune.

wolof: Kuy tëru, kuy teggee ca aay.
variants: Tëru teggee ca aay.
translation: The best way to protect yourself against someone lying in wait for you is to take a different way to him.
explanation: The best way to respond to a menace is to avoid encountering it. If someone tries to offend you, it is best to avoid a conflict by maintaining an honourable conduct. Rather than responding with violence to someone who puts an obstacle in your path, it is best to go around the obstacle.

wolof: Gannaaw dee ga, tuub wees na.
translation: After death, it is too late to repent.
scripture: Just as man is destined to die once, and after that to face judgment. (Hebrews 9:27 NIV) "There was a rich man who was dressed in purple and fine linen and lived in luxury every day. At his gate was laid a beggar named Lazarus, covered with sores and longing to eat what fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores. "The time came when the beggar died and the angels carried him to Abraham’s side. The rich man also died and was buried. In hell, where he was in torment, he looked up and saw Abraham far away, with Lazarus by his side. So he called to him, ‘Father Abraham, have pity on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am in agony in this fire.’ "But Abraham replied, ‘Son, remember that in your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things, but now he is comforted here and you are in agony. And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who want to go from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross over from there to us.’ (Luke 16:19-26 NIV)

wolof: Balaa ngaa dundal ña ca mbedd ma nga dundal ña ca kër ga.
translation: Before you feed those on the street, feed those in your house.
scripture: If anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for his immediate family, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. (1 Timothy 5:8 NIV)

wolof: Gàcce rey na xaj fa béy di màtte gan.
translation: Shame killed the dog where the goat bit the guest.
explanation: Each person in a household or company has his responsibilities. If he neglects them so that others end up doing them he should be ashamed. This proverb is used to rebuke people when they do not fulfil their responsibilities.

wolof: Bu bëy dàqee ab sàcc ci kër, xaj war naa rus.
variants: Bu bëy dàqeeb sàcc ci kër, xaj war naa rus.
translation: When the goat chases away a thief from the house, the dog should be ashamed.
explanation: Each person in a household or company has his responsibilities. If he neglects them so that others end up doing them he should be ashamed. This proverb is used to rebuke people when they do not fulfil their responsibilities.

wolof: Ku tëb ak ay sabaar, dal ak ay gub, soo ko jëlulee it, yow lañu koy jiiñ.
variants: Ku tëb ak i sabaar, daanu ak i gub, su nga leen lekkul, koon it ñu jiiñ la leen.
translation: If you jump with sheaths of millet, and land with several ears, even if you have taken nothing, you will be accused.
scripture: For we are taking pains to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord but also in the eyes of men. (2 Corinthians 8:21 NIV)

wolof: Gàtt-geen, gàtt-geen a koy fey.
variants: Ngatt geen, ngatt geen-a koy fey.
translation: An animal with a short tail must be reimbursed by an animal with a short tail.
explanation: One must recompense another the exact value of the loss. This proverb refers to one of the stories of the hare and hyena.

wolof: Saay-saay ñemewul ku jub.
translation: The bandit dreads the righteous person.

wolof: Sàmm sañ naa maye meew, wànte sañula maye aw sëllu.
translation: The shepherd has the right to offer milk but he does not have the right to offer a calf.
explanation: An employee was generously distributing office materials to his friends to the point where his supervisor noticed. He called him in and rebuked him, quoting this proverb. [Traditionally a shepherd was not paid, but he had the right to profit from the milk from the morning, with the evening’s milk going to the owners.]

wolof: Boroom tubéy, bu jàngoo, sol.
variants: Boroom tubéy saayu jàngoo sol.
translation: The owner of pants, after washing his feet, can wear them.
explanation: The owner has precedence to use what he owns.
scripture: The hardworking farmer should be the first to receive a share of the crops. (2 Timothy 2:6 NIV)

wolof: Jinne su bëggee daqaar, ku yéeg daanu.
variants: Bu jinne bëggee daqaar, ku yéeg daanu.
translation: When the djinn wants a tamarind, whoever climbs (the tamarind tree) will fall.
explanation: One should not compete for something with someone who has a right to the object in question. The person who owns something has precedence over its use. Masylla had promised to loan his donkey to his neighbour. But at the last minute his father-in-law turned up also wanting to borrow the donkey, and Masylla was obliged to give it to him. Embarrassed, Masylla goes to his neighbour to explain the situation and for an excuse quotes this proverb. [The tamarind tree is reputed to be a favourite haunt of evil spirits.]

wolof: Seet seet du tere boroom alal jél alalam.
translation: Coveting what you see will not stop the owner taking what he owns.
scripture: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife. You shall not set your desire on your neighbour’s house or land, his manservant or maidservant, his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbour.” (Deuteronomy 5:21 NIV)

wolof: Fu nag nekk, bukki dee fa.
translation: Where the cows are, it is there that the hyena dies.
explanation: Excessive greed leads the hyena into dangerous situations, i.e. encounters with bulls and herdsmen.

wolof: Lu waay jéemul du ko mën.
translation: No one can do anything if he does not try.
explanation: If you do not try you will not succeed.

wolof: Su may dee, ci àll, gayndee may rey !
variants: Kuy dee ci àll na la gaynde rey.
translation: If I must die in the bush, let it be a lion which kills me.
explanation: The cashier of a company embezzled 110,000 cfa. He was arrested and sentenced to five years in prison. A friend went to visit him and said that he found it ridiculous that he allowed himself to be caught for so small a sum, that if it was him he would not risk prison for anything less than one million. And he quoted this proverb. It is also used to refer to someone with a high social rank who lowers himself to frequent those below his rank.
equivalents: “One might as well be hanged for a sheep as a lamb.”
“In for a penny, in for a pound.”

wolof: Ku bëreey daan.
translation: He who wrestles, wins.

wolof: Sëb, la ko bënn a nga ca biir.
variants: Sëb la, la ko bënn a nga ca biir.
Sëb, li ko mbët a ngi ci biir.
translation: Beans – that which makes holes in them is already inside.
explanation: Many things which are ruined already had the source of ruin within but you could not see it.
scripture: “For what I do is not the good I want to do; no, the evil I do not want to do—this I keep on doing.” (Romans 7:19 NIV)

wolof: Mbamb reyul weer.
variants: Mbamb reytil weer.
translation: Public rumours don't last the month.
explanation: People will gossip about an event for a while then forget about it.

wolof: Bu reer doon doy, reeri daaw ya doy.
translation: If a man could be satisfied with his meal, he would be satisfied by those from last year.
explanation: One is never satisfied with one's lot.

wolof: Ngor moo di lekk suurul, mu jógi.
variants: Ngor moo di lekk suuruloo nga jóg.
translation: Integrity eats but not until full, then leaves the table.
explanation: Integrity only provides the natural self that which is strictly necessary.

wolof: Njullit moo di naan màndiwul, mu bàyyi.
translation: Piety drinks but not until one's thirst is quenched, then leaves it.
explanation: The pious person does not know excess.

wolof: Bukki, balaa baax, yooy.
variants: Bukki, balaa baax, mu yooy.
translation: It is only when the hyena is wasted that he is gentle.
explanation: Someone who has trouble controlling his desires is better off if he does not have the means to get into trouble.

wolof: Bët du yenu, waaye xam na lu bopp àttan.
variants: Bët du yenu, waaye xam na lu bopp antan.
Bët du yenu, wande lu bopp àttan xam na ko.
translation: The eye does not carry a load, but it knows what the head is capable of carrying.
explanation: Everyone is able to judge for himself what his own capabilities are.

wolof: Manees na laa takkal jabar, yóbbul la ko ci sa néeg, waaye il ci des, yow rekk a ko mana def.
translation: One can give you a wife, and bear all the costs to bring her to your home, but the rest only you can do.
explanation: One must learn to depend on oneself, because there will always be situations where one is obliged to deal with a difficulty on one's own.

wolof: Ku ñaan ñàkk, boo jëndee am.
variants: Ku ñaan ñàkk, boo jëndee moom.
translation: What you cannot obtain by begging you will be able to obtain if you pay the price.
explanation: One should rely on oneself, not others, and maintain one's independence through hard work. What one earns for oneself is always better than what one is given.

wolof: Lu la waay maye kon jën, na la ko jàngale napp moo gën.
translation: As good as it is for your friend to give you fish, it is even better for him to teach you to fish.
equivalents: “Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.”

wolof: Gàcce bu reyul semmal.
translation: When shame does not kill you, it does at least harm you.

wolof: Mbañ gàcce.
translation: Avoid shame.

wolof: Bët bu rusul, toj.
variants: Bët bu rusul, tuuru.
translation: The eye which is not sensitive to shame will explode.
explanation: In Wolof society, shame and scruples are the most important factors which condition an individual to submit to the moral and social values of the culture. The person who is not controlled by a sense of shame will inevitably fall in ruin or debauchery.

wolof: Ku amul bopp, na am ay tank.
translation: He who does not have the head (of the sheep) should at least receive a foot.
explanation: He who does not receive the best parts should at least receive something.

wolof: Bët, bu reerul añ.
translation: The eye which doesn't dine, must lunch.
explanation: If you don't get enough sleep during the night you must make it up during the day.
equivalents: “You can’t burn the candle at both ends.”

wolof: Lu jinne màggat màggat, dese ŋelaju bu jommal gone.
variants: Lu jinne màggat màggat, dese regeju bu jommal ndaw.
translation: A djinn, no matter how old it is, is still capable of making faces that panic children.
explanation: Experience will triumph over strength. Bismi Ndoye, a wrestler in his nineties, attracted by the importance of the stakes, accepts a challenge to confront Bori Diouf, a young wrestler who is a champion in all categories, in a wrestling match. Following the signal to start the match, Bismi refused contact with his adversary, all the time playing the clown, doubling over towards the crowd with laughter. Eventually Bori is exasperated and forces Bismi to fight hand to hand. Bismi gets a good grip, and at the moment when Bori wants to unbalance him, he sticks a finger in the bottom of his back. Bori jumps and Bismi trips him up and thus gets the victory. Bori complains to the umpire who did not see anything, to no avail. At the moment of the final accolade after the match, Bismi whispers this proverb into the ear of Bori. [ŋeleju = to make faces at someone with the goal of offending or demoralising them. regeju = to roll one's eyes in an expressive manner.]

wolof: Tepp-tepp ay yóbbu cim xuus.
variants: Tepp-tepp ay indim xuus.
Tepp-teppal mooy indi xuus.
translation: A small puddle will lead to wading through water.
explanation: One should not despise small things. They can end up being very important.
equivalents: “From little streams, great rivers are formed.”
scripture: “Who despises the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10 NIV)

wolof: Ku amul kilifa, jinne doon sa kilifa !
variants: Ku nanguwul nit yilif la, jinne doon sa kilifa.
translation: He who does not take a human being as his (religious) teacher, the devil will be his teacher.
explanation: This stresses the role of society in moulding the individual and establishing moral values. Anyone who rejects submission to the values of society will inevitably end up in debauchery.
scripture: “You will say, "How I hated discipline! How my heart spurned correction! I would not obey my teachers or listen to my instructors. I have come to the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly."” (Proverbs 5:12-14 NIV)

wolof: Bala ngay tuufu, teppalil.
translation: Before you put drops in your eye, separate the eyelids.
explanation: One should not do things in the wrong order.
equivalents: “Don't put the cart before the horse.”

wolof: Ñàkk pexe, pexe la.
translation: Even the wildest of solutions is a solution.

wolof: Pexe du jeex.
translation: There are no end of solutions.

wolof: Dindi, loo fa defoon a ca gën.
variants: Dindi, la nga defoon a ca gën.
translation: It's easier to undo yourself what you have already done.
explanation: It takes less time to solve a problem that you already know the solution to.

wolof: Guddi am na boroom.
translation: The night has a master.
explanation: The night belongs to supernatural beings. This proverb is used for those who scorn the popular belief that djinn inhabit the night and therefore it is unwise to be out late at night or leave before the predawn call of the mosque.
scripture: “Since the children have flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity so that by his death he might destroy him who holds the power of death—that is, the devil—” (Hebrews 2:14 NIV)
“And having disarmed the powers and authorities, he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.” (Colossians 2:15 NIV)

wolof: Jëkk a fecc taxul a mujjeb géew.
translation: Being the first dancer doesn't mean you'll be the last dancer in the circle.
explanation: To be the first to do something does not mean that you are better or more important than others. You can lead in a group but that doesn't mean you're going to be the only leader. [mujjeb géew = mujje ab géew]

wolof: Doxandéem nelawul ba yàndoor.
translation: A stranger does not sleep soundly.

wolof: Bukki bu daanee ponkal ca doxin wa la.
variants: Bukki, bu songee ponkal ca doxin wa la.
translation: If an hyena manages to defeat a giant/lion it is because of his (imposing) appearance.
explanation: Mamoussé Diagne explains that the hyena is an animal characterised by cowardice. How does a coward defeat a giant? When the giant deprecates himself so much that the hyena has the courage to attack. When a person acts in a way that is unworthy then he sets himself up to be defeated by anyone who comes along. When you lie down somewhere, it is your own fault if people step on you. An imposing or frightening appearance can contribute to the success of a venture.
scripture: “Be self-controlled and alert. Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour.” (1 Peter 5:8 NIV)

wolof: Bu bukki dabee gaynde, ca doxin wa la.
variants: Bukki su yabee gaynde ca doxin wa la.
translation: If an hyena manages to defeat a giant/lion it is because of his (imposing) appearance.
explanation: Mamoussé Diagne explains that the hyena is an animal characterised by cowardice. How does a coward defeat a giant? When the giant deprecates himself so much that the hyena has the courage to attack. When a person acts in a way that is unworthy then he sets himself up to be defeated by anyone who comes along. wolof: Boroom lal a xam i màttam.
variants: Tëddji lal, moo xam ay màttam.
Boroom lal a xam màttu lalam.
translation: The owner of a bed is best placed to speak of his bedbugs.
explanation: Only the person who experiences suffering knows the pain.
equivalents: “Before you criticize someone, walk a mile in his shoes.”
scripture: “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathise with our weaknesses, but we have one who has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet was without sin.” (Hebrews 4:15 NIV)

wolof: Garab gu la sutul, du la may ker.
translation: A tree, if it is not taller than you, won't give you shade.
explanation: Meaning, before you can teach someone or help someone, you must first have something you have learned to offer them which will help them. Someone who has not surpassed you in some domain cannot help you.

wolof: Ku la sut nee ko njool mi.
variants: Ku la sut, nga ne ko njool mi.
translation: You should call someone who is taller than you “tall”.
explanation: You should admit it when someone is better than you, and fall behind him in the areas where he surpasses you.

wolof: Ku la jëkka yeewu ne la sàngul.
variants: Ku la jëkka yeewu, ne la sàngal say taat.
translation: The one who wakes up before you will tell you to cover your butt.
explanation: If someone has an advantage over you, he will manipulate you. Someone who applies himself better than you, or has been working longer than you, who has contributed more than you ends up with results or experience that you don't have. He therefore gains the authority to highlight your insufficiencies if necessary.

wolof: Lu la sutul, du la mana may ker.
variants: Lu la sutul manu laa keral.
translation: Someone who is not taller than you cannot give you shade.
explanation: Someone who is not better off than you cannot help you. If you want a protector you have to seek someone who is more powerful than you are.

wolof: Lu la bett, mën la.
translation: Anything which takes you by surprise is stronger than you.

wolof: Lu la mar mayul, màtt du la ko may.
translation: Whatever you cannot get by licking you will not get by biting.
explanation: Tact and diplomacy are the only successful means of influencing people. Whatever you cannot get by kindness, diplomacy, politeness and courtesy you will not get through violence, or meanness. Kumba asks her husband, Modu for 110,000 cfa in order to buy a bracelet. He tells her that it will not be possible for 19 months. However she thinks that the delay is just an excuse. For a whole week she is extremely nice but speaks every time of the bracelet. When her goodness does not shake up the resolution of Modu, she loses the passion she had during the evenings of the previous week, then she becomes positively cold, and then aggressive. Seeing their harmony deterioriating Modu finishes by telling her this proverb.

wolof: Lu la yar ak teggin mayul, leneen du la ko may.
translation: What you cannot get with politeness and courtesy, you will not get by any other means.
explanation: Tact and diplomacy are the only successful means of influencing people. Whatever you cannot get by kindness, diplomacy, politeness and courtesy you will not get through violence, or meanness. Kumba asks her husband, Modu for 110,000 cfa in order to buy a bracelet. Seeing their harmony deterioriating Modu finishes by telling her this proverb.

wolof: Lu bëñ bu weex mayewul bu xuur du ko maye.
translation: What you don't get with a nice smile, you won't get with a grim one.
explanation: Tact and diplomacy are the only successful means of influencing people. Whatever you cannot get by kindness, diplomacy, politeness and courtesy you will not get through violence, or meanness. Kumba asks her husband, Modu for 110,000 cfa in order to buy a bracelet. Seeing their harmony deterioriating Modu finishes by telling her this proverb.

wolof: Lu la raay mayul, wokk du la ko may.
translation: Whatever you cannot get by caresses you will not get by scratching.
explanation: Tact and diplomacy are the only successful means of influencing people. Whatever you cannot get by kindness, diplomacy, politeness and courtesy you will not get through violence, or meanness. Kumba asks her husband, Modu for 110,000 cfa in order to buy a bracelet. He tells her that it will not be possible for 19 months. However she thinks that the delay is just an excuse. For a whole week she is extremely nice but speaks every time of the bracelet. When her goodness does not shake up the resolution of Modu, she loses the passion she had during the evenings of the previous week, then she becomes positively cold, and then aggressive. Seeing their harmony deterioriating Modu finishes by telling her this proverb.

wolof: “Ayca nañu ko def” joo gis, “ayca nañu ko wax” a ko jiitu.
variants: “Ayca nañ(u) ko def” joo gis, “ayca nañ(u) ko waxtaanee” wara jiitu.
“Na nu def” joo gis, “na nu wax” a ko jëkk.
translation: Every “Let us do it” that you hear was preceded by “Let us talk”.
explanation: Action should be preceded by discussion and agreement.

wolof: Ku wax feeñ.
translation: Whoever speaks gives himself away.
scripture: “The good man brings good things out of the good stored up in his heart, and the evil man brings evil things out of the evil stored up in his heart. For out of the overflow of his heart his mouth speaks.” (Luke 6:45 NIV)

wolof: Ay wax yu bare, du may lu ñu lekk.
translation: Much talk does not provide food.
scripture: Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to him, “Go, I wish you well; keep warm and well fed,” but does nothing about his physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead. But someone will say, “You have faith; I have deeds.” Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by what I do. (James 2:15-18 NIV)

wolof: Bu wax neexul, tontu du mën a neex.
translation: If the word is unpleasant, then the reply cannot be pleasant.
explanation: If you want someone to speak pleasantly, you need to speak pleasantly.
scripture: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1 NIV)

wolof: Gajjug xuloo, dëkk bu mu sax, sémmiñu waxtaan a koy gor.
translation: The thicket of dispute, in the village where it sprouts, is cut down by the axe of discussion.

wolof: Ki wax, waxul ; ki jottali moo wax.
translation: It is not the person who first said it who said it. It is the person who transmitted it who said it.
explanation: The person who serves as the agent to transmit a statement is often considered to be the source.

wolof: Ku waxul, sa xumbal du fey.
translation: He who does not speak, his pipe does not go out.
explanation: This proverb is said to make it known that one refuses to speak in order to put an end to an argument.
scripture: “A fool shows his annoyance at once, but a prudent man overlooks an insult.” (Proverbs 12:16 NIV)
“Even a fool is thought wise if he keeps silent, and discerning if he holds his tongue.” (Proverbs 17:28 NIV)

wolof: Ku xamoon lu ñu lay tontu bala ngaa wax, waaj ko.
translation: If you knew how people would reply to you, you would be more careful in what you say.

wolof: Lu nekk mënees na koo toxal, mu mel na mu meloon ba mu des wax.
translation: One can move anything without changing it except words.
explanation: It is not possible to pass on the words of someone else without changing them.

wolof: Na góor aay biir, wànde bu mu aay làmmiñ.
translation: A person can have bad feelings inside but he should not show it by his words.
scripture: “A fool gives full vent to his anger, but a wise man keeps himself under control.” (Proverbs 29:11 NIV)

wolof: Ku tëb di wax, doo noppee juum.
translation: Whoever speaks without thinking will make many errors.

wolof: Nit ku baax dey xam lu bari, wax lu néew.
translation: The good man knows much but says little.
scripture: “A prudent man keeps his knowledge to himself, but the heart of fools blurts out folly.” (Proverbs 12:23 NIV)
“Wisdom reposes in the heart of the discerning and even among fools she lets herself be known.” (Proverbs 14:33 NIV)
“Wise men store up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool invites ruin.” (Proverbs 10:14 NIV)
“The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouth of the fool gushes folly.” (Proverbs 15:2 NIV)

wolof: Wax ju neex sarax la.
translation: Good words are like an offering to the poor.
explanation: To know how to speak well is of great value.
scripture: “A word aptly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” (Proverbs 25:11 NIV)

wolof: Wax, su guddee, ñaar a ko guddal.
translation: It takes two people for a dispute to last for a long time.
equivalents: “It takes two to quarrel, but only one to end it.”

wolof: Wax ju bari, wax ju néew te wér a ko gën.
translation: It is better to say little which is certain than to say much.
scripture: “Even a fool is thought wise if he keeps silent, and discerning if he holds his tongue.” (Proverbs 17:28 NIV)

wolof: Wax, soxu fetal la, su rëccee, dabu ko wees.
translation: A word is like a loaded rifle. If it goes off, it cannot be taken back.
scripture: “Likewise the tongue is a small part of the body, but it makes great boasts. Consider what a great forest is set on fire by a small spark. The tongue also is a fire, a world of evil among the parts of the body. It corrupts the whole person, sets the whole course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.” (James 3:5-6 NIV)

wolof: Wax, ab xottiku la, kenn ku ne, yaa xam noo koy ñawe.
translation: A dispute is like a tear. It is up to each person to determine how he will repair it.

wolof: Waxin la déggin la laaj.
translation: For allusive speech you need an allusive ear.
explanation: Speeches, proverbs and folk stories are filled with hidden meanings.

wolof: Fu jàmm yendu nit a fa xam lu mu waxul.
variants: Fu jàmm yendu, waay a fa xam lu mu waxul.
translation: Where peace reigns there is someone who knows something he has not said.
explanation: There is no peace if one says everything one knows about others.

wolof: Xam lépp, wax lépp, baaxul.
translation: To know everything and say everything is bad.

wolof: “Waxoon naa koo” gën “xamoon naa ko”.
variants: Magum waxoon naa ko moo gën magum xamoon naa ko.
Duma magum xamoon naa ko, wànte magum waxoon naa ko.
translation: “I told you that” is better than “I knew that”.
explanation: It is better to have warned someone of a problem than to have been aware of it and said nothing.
scripture: “Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil on my head. My head will not refuse it. Yet my prayer is ever against the deeds of evildoers;” (Psalms 141:5 NIV)
“Do not rebuke a mocker or he will hate you; rebuke a wise man and he will love you.” (Proverbs 9:8 NIV)

wolof: Buy, balaa jëriñ, toj.
variants: Wuy, balaa jëriñ, toj.
translation: Before the fruit of a baobab tree is of any use it must be broken.
explanation: A person can only use what he knows. If you do not speak your thoughts, your advice or your needs, then someone cannot respond to them.

wolof: La mu saf, ka ko macc a ko xam.
translation: Only the person who actually tastes it will know what it tastes like.
explanation: One cannot criticize what one does not understand. Only the person who has tasted and understood can be critical of others. Every week Iba sees M. Dupont coming to his village to chase butterflies. Iba, who finds this past-time somewhat trivial, says to Abdou one day, “This guy is bizarre. To come such a long distance, burn up so much fuel just to run behind butterflies! Ah these Tubaabs!” But instead of laughing Abdou quotes this proverb.

wolof: Loo doonul ndongoom doo doon ub sëriñam.
variants: Loo nekkul taalibeem doo nekkub sëriñam.
translation: If you have not been a disciple you will not be a teacher.
explanation: What you have not been taught you will not be able to teach.

wolof: Yéene néeg la, boroom a cay fanaan.
translation: A wish is a bedroom; the person who forms it will pass the night in it.
explanation: A wish (good or bad) and the thoughts that one has towards another is like a boomerang. A blessing or curse will come back on the head of the person who makes it.
equivalents: “Curses, like chickens, come home to roost.”
scripture: “Do not judge, or you too will be judged. For in the same way as you judge others, you will be judged, and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you.” (Matthew 7:1-2 NIV)

wolof: Yàgg du saabu, waaye dana fóot.
translation: Time is not soap but it can wash the dirty washing.
explanation: With time, the truth always manifests itself. A stranger arrived in a village in which lives a man with a reputation for wisdom and honesty. Everywhere he went he heard people mention this man but hesitated to believe all that was said of him. One day he shared his scepticism with someone, who told him he would end up being convinced, and quoted this proverb. An honest man was accused of taking something that didn't belong to him. Although he proclaimed his innocence no one believed him. He continued to proclaim his innocence, quoting this proverb.

wolof: Yàggaay dindi tuuma.
translation: Time clears accusations.
explanation: Over time people can see whether or not what someone has been accused of is true or not.

wolof: Ku wàcc sa and, and boo war mu toj.
translation: Whoever abandons his incense pot will find that other incense pots will break wherever he sits on them.
explanation: Whoever denies his origins or the traditions with which he grew up ends up on a path of permanent imbalance as he will never be able to adapt himself to other traditions and environments.

wolof: Ku wacc sa and, and boo dem fekk boroom toog ca.
variants: And bu mu dem fekk fa boroom.
Ku wacc sa and, and boo dem fekk ca boroom.
Ku wacc sab and, and boo dem fekk fa boroom.
translation: Whoever abandons his incense pot will find that everywhere he goes the incense pots are already occupied by others.
explanation: You should hold onto your values because it's very difficult to get someone else's values.

wolof: Doxkat du fekke deewug baay ba.
translation: One who travels too much will not be present at his father's death.
explanation: If you never stay somewhere long enough, you will always miss important events. According to Sylla this pejorative proverb indicates a person who does not undertake his share of family responsibilities, thus he does not defend his heritage. To know how to 'travel' for a man, is to move for useful purposes – to act as an intermediary, to settle differences.

wolof: Ku yàgg dox, yàgg gis.
translation: He who travels for a long time sees a lot.
explanation: Travelling gives experience.

wolof: Àddina, ndoxum joor la ; buy taa, mu ngay ŋiis.
translation: The things of this world are comparable to water on a sandy plane; no sooner has it spread over the sand than it infiltrates and disappears.
explanation: The things of this world are only temporary, We should therefore make preparations for our eventual deaths by a detachment from things of this world, self-control over one's passions and by doing good works.
scripture: “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy, and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Matthew 6:19-21 NIV)

wolof: Àddina ak li ci biiram jarul a xiirook a ŋaayoo.
translation: The world and all its wealth are not worth quarrelling over and falling out with someone.
explanation: You should not let yourself be led by material belongings to fight like cats and dogs.
scripture: “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs.” (1 Timothy 6:10 NIV)

wolof: Alal joo gis, alaa ka fa ba.
translation: The treasure that you see, “no” will see that it is left there.
explanation: This proverb is a mixture of Pulaar and Wolof. alaa is “no” in Pulaar. So the expression is in expanded form Alal joo gis déedéet moo ko fa bàyyi. It is said when someone asks for something to say that they can't have it.

wolof: Alalu jaambur ba la sant.
variants: Alalu jaambur ba fa la sant.
translation: Someone else’s treasure has as its surname “leave it alone”.
explanation: This proverb is a play on words between the verb ba meaning to leave something alone, and the Fula family name Ba.

wolof: Alalu golo : ca lex ba.
translation: All the treasures of a monkey are found in his cheeks.
explanation: One keeps things of value close to oneself.

wolof: Am saxul, ñàkk it saxul.
translation: Possessions do not last; and neither does destitution.
explanation: Riches and poverty do not last long. With time both will pass.

wolof: Barile, baaxlee ko gën.
translation: It is better to have something good than something in abundance.
explanation: Having something useful, even if it is lacking in quantity, is better than having much of something of little use.

wolof: Ku moomul sa alal, sa alal moom la.
translation: If you do not master your wealth, you will become its slave.
explanation: Riches become a kind of bondage for those who do not know how to handle them with wisdom.

wolof: Bu la am-am tax a bew, ndax nàkk du wees.
translation: Don't let your possessions cause you to become conceited and self-satisfied because you can always lose them.
scripture: “Do not trust in extortion or take pride in stolen goods; though your riches increase, do not set your heart on them.” (Psalms 62:10 NIV)
“Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will thrive like a green leaf.” (Proverbs 11:28 NIV)
“Dishonest money dwindles away, but he who gathers money little by little makes it grow.” (Proverbs 13:11 NIV)

wolof: Li gën a jafe ci àddina mooy am alal ju ne gàññ, lew domm.
translation: The hardest thing in the world is to have great wealth acquired completely honestly.

wolof: Nit ay liggéey alal, waaye alal du liggéey nit.
translation: Man should work his riches; his riches should not work him.

wolof: Alal fajul dee, gàcce lay faj.
variants: Alal du faj dee, gàcce lay faj.
translation: One's wealth does not prevent one from dying, but it can solve your immediate problems which would bring shame.
explanation: If you own something, in the face of need, sell it to solve your problem and avoid facing shame. As long as you are still living and are in need, sell what you own to solve your problem and thereby avoid facing shame.

wolof: Alal yu bare, yaram wu wér a ko gën.
translation: Good health is more important than many riches.
scripture: “A good name is more desirable than great riches; to be esteemed is better than silver or gold.” (Proverbs 22:1 NIV)

wolof: Béy du gëmal gënn.
translation: A goat will never believe that a mortar is empty.
explanation: You will not believe when you are told that you can no longer have something you are used to having.

wolof: Bukki, kenn du ko dénk ay seel.
variants: Kenn du dénk Bukki ay seel.
translation: No one entrusts an hyena with strips of dried meat.
explanation: Don't entrust someone with things that they particularly want themselves.
equivalents: “Don’t put the fox in charge of the chicken coop.”

wolof: Ak lu nar teel a xéy, bu dëgg gontee, jot ko.
translation: However early a lie sets out, even if truth sets out in the evening, it will catch up with it.
explanation: Truth always wins out.

wolof: Lu nar barey barey su dëgg jógee jot ko.
translation: Lies, however numerous, will be caught by truth when it rises up.

wolof: Baatu dëgg yomb naa xam.
translation: The voice of truth is easy to know.

wolof: Bu caaxaan wéyee, dëgg a des.
translation: When the joking around has passed, truth will remain.

wolof: Dëgg du yendu àll, fanaan fa.
translation: Truth having spent the day in the wilderness will not also pass the night.
explanation: Truth might be slow to come home but come home it will. The truth always eventually reveals itself.

wolof: Fukki nit mënuñoo bokk fen.
translation: Ten people cannot share a lie.

wolof: Gémmiñ gu waxul dëgg wax fen.
translation: The mouth which does not speak the truth, speaks lies.

wolof: Làmmiñu luu a gën làmmiñu fenkat.
translation: The tongue of a mute person is better than that of a liar.

wolof: Lëkkale ay fen taxula am dëgg.
translation: Lining up a series of lies does not put the truth on your side.

wolof: Lu dul dëgg du yàgg.
translation: That which is not true won't last.
scripture: “Truthful lips endure for ever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment.” (Proverbs 12:19 NIV)

wolof: Saay-saay waxul dëgg, waaye yàq nam xel.
variants: Saay-saay waxul dëgg, waaye yàq na xol.
Seytaane waxul dëgg waaye yàq nay xalaat.
translation: The lout does not tell the truth, but he does trouble hearts.
explanation: The treacherous create doubt by their lies.

wolof: Yàgg ay wone légétub taat.
translation: It is with time that one discovers scars on someone's backside.
explanation: Time reveals the hidden aspects of something. A person's true character will only become evident with the passage of time. Guilaye rents a room privately. He initially presented himself as friendly and helpful to all the family. He was particularly kind with the children, and tolerated their din in his room. Everyone appreciated him. However after several months he began spending less and less time talking with the family and was not longer available to help. Several times he even got angry with the children and chased them from his room. The grandfather told someone who was surprised by the change in attitude that his real character had come to light and quotes this proverb.

wolof: Dëgg a neex Yàlla.
translation: Only the truth pleases God.
explanation: This is usually said before telling someone an unpleasant truth.
scripture: “He is the Rock, his works are perfect, and all his ways are just. A faithful God who does no wrong, upright and just is he.” (Deuteronomy 32:4 NIV)
“Surely you desire truth in the inner parts; you teach me wisdom in the inmost place.” (Psalms 51:6 NIV)

wolof: Dëgg, puso bu réer la : gune man na ko for, mag man na ko for.
variants: Dëgg, puso bu réer la : mag dana ko for, ndaw dana ko for.
translation: The truth/wisdom/knowledge is like a lost needle: a child could pick it up just as easily as an adult.
explanation: One says this when a child happens to say a truth which surprises an adult.

wolof: Xel, puso bu réer la, mag dina ko for, xale dina ko for.
translation: The truth/wisdom/knowledge is like a lost needle: a child could pick it up just as easily as an adult.
explanation: One says this when a child happens to say a truth which surprises an adult.

wolof: Xam-xam, puso bu réer la, mag dina ko for, xale dina ko for.
translation: The truth/wisdom/knowledge is like a lost needle: a child could pick it up just as easily as an adult.
explanation: One says this when a child happens to say a truth which surprises an adult.

wolof: Dëgg, kaani la, ku ñu ko xëpp nga toxoñu.
variants: Dëgg kaani la, koo ko tuuf mu toxoñu.
translation: The truth is like chilli. If it is thrown in your face, you will rub your eyes.
explanation: Truth hurts. The truth is not always pleasant to hear.
scripture: “Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will in all things grow up into him who is the Head, that is, Christ.” (Ephesians 4:15 NIV)
“Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses.” (Proverbs 27:6 NIV)

wolof: Fen wuy defarug mbokk a gën dëgg gu koy yàq.
variants: Fen wuy defar moo gën dëgg guy yàq.
translation: A lie that reconciles people is better to a truth that puts them apart.
explanation: If you know of someone, something which can be hidden to another person or family, whom knowing about it can break their relationship with that particular person, it's better to keep that truth to yourself.

wolof: Bukki nee : “Li ñépp wax ay dëgg !”
variants: Li ñépp wax ay dëgg.
translation: The hyena says “What everyone says must be the truth!”
explanation: What most people say will be believed as being true. The hyena is often quoted as a source of wisdom.

wolof: “Sa gémmiñ xasaw na”, sa doomu-ndey a la koy wax.
variants: “Sa gémmiñ gi xasaw na” sa mbokk a la koy wax.
translation: Only your close relative can tell you that you have bad breath.
explanation: One should not take offence at what such a relative says. But a cross-cousin equally well has a duty to criticize when necessary, and say what it would be offensive for others to say. Because he cares, a close relative might tell you an unpleasant truth.

wolof: Geenub géléem sàngul uw taat te dàqul i weñ.
translation: The tail of a camel cannot cover its rear nor chase away flies.
explanation: Diéri is short of money. He does the rounds of his relatives in the village but in vain. He hopes that his best friend, Baidi, will be able to help him out of his difficulties. Even though Baidi lives in a village far away, he goes to visit him. Baidi cannot do much to help Dieri apart from giving him a little to help pay for his fare to return home. When Dieri gets home he tells his wife that not only was Baidi unable to give him what he hoped for but he could not even pay a half of his travel costs, and he cites this proverb.

wolof: Ku yëy yaxub bukki, yëy na yaxub yëykatu yax.
variants: Ku yëy yaxi bukki, yëy nga yaxi yëykat.
translation: Whoever chews on the bones of an hyena, you are chewing on the bones of someone who chews bone.
explanation: Defeating a champion wrestler does not mean he is not a champion.

wolof: Lu sakkantalkat ba denc, sallaxkat ba sànni.
translation: That which the miser saves, the prodigal will fritter away.

wolof: Nit a ngay jëggaani lu ni gàññ ca péeyam.
translation: A person travels very far to seek for something which is in abundance in his own capital.
explanation: There is no need to go very far if you want to learn wisdom.

wolof: Xel du doy.
variants: Benn xel doyul.
translation: One cannot have enough advice. One mind is not enough.

wolof: Xel koomum boroom la.
translation: Wisdom is the resource/wealth of its owner.

wolof: “Yàlla, Yàlla”, bey sa tool.
translation: Pray to God, but cultivate your field.
explanation: It is not enough to simply rely on God, and ignore one's responsibilities. One must also work.

wolof: Bala nga am dara, nga wiccaxndiku sa nàq.
translation: Before you have something, you must shake off your sweat with your fingers.
explanation: One must be willing to work and make sacrifices in order to have something.

wolof: Bu mbey matee faj baaraam des.
translation: When the work in the fields is finished, all that is left is to treat the fingers.
explanation: One cannot achieve a task without suffering the sacrifices which the task entails.

wolof: Farala liggéey dina sawarloo.
translation: To be in a habit of working makes one eager.

wolof: Ku bëgg xaalis, liggéey.
translation: He who loves money must labour.

wolof: Ku biddante, xiif.
translation: He who sleeps late will go hungry.
explanation: Laziness brings poverty. Prov 6:11-12; 24:33-34
scripture: “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest— and poverty will come on you like a bandit and scarcity like an armed man.” (Proverbs 6:10-11; 24:33-34 NIV)

wolof: Ku sawar ci liggéey, oomle.
translation: Whoever works with eagerness will be wealthy.

wolof: Ku sonn, jëriñoo.
translation: One profits from difficulties and tiredness.
explanation: There is no success without effort and trouble.

wolof: Liggéey bu amulug pey, yàgg lay taawloo, caatloo bon.
translation: Work without pay, if it first gives birth to a long time, it finally gives birth to evil.
explanation: If you do not pay your worker what pleases him, he will not do work that pleases you.

wolof: Mbey bey a koy jeexal.
translation: Only working the field can finish the season.
explanation: A farmer will only reap the rewards of his fields through his sweat. A task not yet carried out will remain incomplete until someone gets out and does the work.

wolof: Nit mënul lekk lu gën li mu liggéey ci loxol boppam.
translation: A person cannot eat anything better than that which he has worked for with his own hands.

wolof: Ñaq jariñu, jëf jël.
translation: Sweat and profit; act and take.
explanation: A person will eventually profit from the sweat that hard work brings. One must accept the need to act and work hard to be successful.

wolof: Toolu golo du meññ.
variants: Toolu golo du ñor.
translation: The field of a monkey will not bear fruit.
explanation: Bara is a shopkeeper. He has a well-situated shop and regular customers, but every time he makes a profit, he buys a sheep and invites all his friends to a feast. Eventually, his extravagance put his business in peril. One day at a family reunion, a cousin remarked that the shop was almost empty of stock. An uncle, in order to comment, quotes this proverb.

wolof: Su liggéey mettee, setal mpey ma.
translation: If the work is difficult, keep in mind the pay.

wolof: Lu dul raaf amul ci àddina si.
translation: There is nothing in this world that does not eventually perish.
scripture: “The world and its desires pass away, but the man who does the will of God lives for ever.” (1 John 2:17 NIV)
